entries.title: Microschooling has grown in Illinois. Here’s what it's like for one Chicago teacher and south suburban mom
entries.summary: <p>A couple years ago, Ollie Allen had offers for two full-time teaching positions sitting on her desk.</p><p>She’d spent time substitute teaching at two public elementary schools in Chicago, one run by the district and the other by a charter network. At both, she was known for her ability to ease challenging behavior and work with students who need one-on-one support.</p><p>But Allen made the daring decision to decline both offers and instead open up her own “microschool” — an education model outside of traditional school systems that’s <a class="Link" href="https://stateline.org/2025/08/08/microschools-are-growing-in-popularity-but-state-regulations-havent-caught-up/" target="_blank" ><u>growing across the country</u></a>.</p><p>“I felt like too many kids were being left behind,” Allen said of the schools where she’d worked.</p><p>Microschooling took off in the early days of the pandemic, when schools offered little or no in-person instruction and parents went in search of other options for their children. <a class="Link" href="https://www.usnews.com/education/k12/articles/what-is-a-microschool" target="_blank" ><u>The model has persisted</u></a>, and researchers estimate that nationally, between 1 and 2 million school-age children are enrolled in microschools, <a class="Link" href="https://www.rand.org/pubs/research_reports/RRA3698-1.html" target="_blank" ><u>according to a 2025 report</u></a> from the RAND Corporation, a nonprofit research organization. That’s on par with the number of students enrolled in K-12 Catholic schools.</p><p>Though there’s no standard definition of a microschool, these programs tend to be small, with around 15 students or less. They typically include multiple grades in the same class and offer lessons that cater to individual students’ interests and learning styles, as opposed to standardized curricula. Microschools often charge tuition and can operate as private schools, homeschools or private businesses.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Microschools tend to be small and include students at different grade levels. They can offer students the chance to learn lessons tailored to their interests and needs, but in Illinois they often operate as homeschools with little state oversight.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Kameron Clepper/For the Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>The size of the movement varies widely, depending on factors like state legislation and private school regulations, according to Don Soifer of the National Microschooling Center. Microschools have exploded in popularity in states like Florida and Arizona, where school choice programs <a class="Link" href="https://www.fldoe.org/schools/school-choice/k-12-scholarship-programs/ftc/pep-faqs.stml" target="_blank" ><u>have expanded</u></a> in recent years and <a class="Link" href="https://www.azed.gov/esa" target="_blank" ><u>now allow families</u></a> to put state scholarship funds toward microschool tuition.</p><p>The microschooling movement exists but isn’t as robust in Illinois, a state with strict private school regulations and more limited school choice programs, says Soifer.</p><p>It’s unclear how many microschools exist in Illinois. Many operate as homeschools with no state oversight and <a class="Link" href="https://www.isbe.net/Pages/Homeschool.aspx" target="_blank" ><u>few requirements</u></a> — namely that they must teach six key subjects, including language arts and math.</p><p>In 2025, the National Microschooling Center surveyed 800 microschools across the U.S. and found that nearly three-quarters serve neurodivergent students and about half serve children who’ve experienced emotional trauma or have other special needs.</p><p>Melissa Feiger, a microschool founder based in Lincoln Park, runs a program specifically for neurodivergent students. A former public school teacher, Feiger hopes that public schools take note of the personalization and flexibility that microschools can offer.</p><p>“Every kid deserves this type of education,” she said. “They should enjoy learning, they should want to come to school and feel safe. And that’s what microschools are doing right now. We’re showing the traditional system what it could look like.”</p><h3>Ollie Allen, founder of Teach Them How to Learn, a microschool in Hyde Park</h3><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Ollie Allen, of Teach Them How to Learn, looks out of her classroom window at the Hyde Park Neighborhood Club in late October.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Kameron Clepper/For the Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Allen got the inspiration to open her Chicago microschool while she was teaching in Las Vegas. She saw that her students needed more support, so she started offering after-school and summer tutoring. As she worked with third to fifth graders outside the constraints of a typical school day, she realized she could take a different approach to education.</p><p>“Doing the all-day summer program was a full day of learning. And it was so fun,” Allen said. “I saw the light bulbs going off in the kids’ eyes. I saw growth and progress. I saw kids helping other kids to get ideas… That was the picture that I needed to see that this could work.”</p><p>After moving back home to Chicago, she opened Teach Them How to Learn, a microschool that now serves seven students in Hyde Park, including two of her own children. Monthly tuition costs $700. Her students range in age from 8 to 13, and every day looks a little different. On Mondays, students often focus on learning new academic material, while on Wednesdays they engage in hands-on learning, such as culinary activities.</p><p>One of the biggest perks of microschooling, she says, is the ability to be flexible in how she teaches — to go outside for a nature lesson one day and take a field trip to a museum on another.</p><p>“We’re not stuck to one particular curriculum, we’re not stuck in one particular room, we’re not stuck trying to get ready for a test,” Allen said.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Her small class size allows Ollie Allen to tailor lessons to her students’ unique interests and needs. If a student is interested in trees, they might learn biology through lessons about nature.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Kameron Clepper/For the Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Every student learns according to an individualized plan. She assesses each student on the skills expected from a child at their grade level using observations and the online learning platform IXL, and then designs a curriculum that may span multiple grade levels.</p><p>Allen incorporates each student’s interests as much as possible. If one child is particularly interested in trees, for instance, she might teach subjects like biology and social studies using nature lessons. Another child with different interests would have lessons that look different. Her goal is for “every kid to feel special at the end of the day and feel like they’re learning at their level,” she said.</p><p>The small class size allows her to come up with these individualized plans. It’s a big difference from how she approached lesson planning in public school, where she often had to break down the same material for many students learning at very different paces.</p><p>“It actually takes me less time to plan for each student than it did when I was in public school,” she said.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> She points to one fifth grader who came into her program last year reading at a kindergarten level and doing first-grade math.</p><p>Since then, they’ve made a lot of progress, she said, and are at a fourth grade level in both subjects. They just needed more support, Allen said, and a school setting where they could “practice different subjects multiple times over and over again.”</p><p>Still, there are challenges. For one, the path is not as financially secure as teaching in a school district or private school. More than once, she’s had parents show interest in enrolling their children, only to back out as the school year approached, leaving Allen with a smaller income than she expected.</p><p>Regardless, Allen continues to promote the program and, like Feiger, believes teachers in traditional classrooms could learn from the microschooling model.</p><p>“My goal is to educate future educators on skills that are unique to microschooling, but beneficial for classrooms, too,” she said.</p><h3>LaToya Jackson, a parent who chose a south suburban microschool for her daughter</h3><div class="Enhancement" Mahogany.</p><p>After missing preschool due to the pandemic, Mahogany was behind her peers at a Catholic school in Chicago’s south suburbs. Through kindergarten and into first grade, Mahogany struggled to keep up with her class. She was soon having behavioral issues, like trying to leave the classroom without permission, that Jackson hadn’t seen before.</p><p>When she went to the school for help, Jackson was told that Mahogany needed an individualized education program, or an IEP — a learning plan outlining support and accommodations for students with disabilities that’s legally required in public schools. Private schools, on the other hand, are not required to provide them, Jackson learned.</p><p>“They just said that they don’t do IEPs,” Jackson recalled. “They don’t do specialized learning. The classroom is the classroom. Either the kid keeps up or they don’t. And that was pretty much it.”</p><p>Jackson and her husband didn’t know much about the public schools in their area, and they were interested in other options. Through her research, Jackson came across Freestyle Learning, a microschool in south suburban Forest Park that doubles as a support center “for families that want to homeschool, but can’t,” according to their website. said. “She no longer has to fake it and act as if she's reading a book. Because now, she knows she’s excited to read.”</p><p>Jackson has noticed that her daughter is more capable of completing assignments independently. She credits the one-on-one help from Thomas paired with opportunities for Mahogany to learn at her own pace.</p><p>But she’s also seen the drawbacks of microschooling. She worries that her daughter isn’t getting a sense of the “real world” — she attends school Monday to Thursday, and now thinks that Fridays are days off, for example.</p><p>Jackson is weighing whether to transfer her daughter to a traditional school in a couple years to see how she does. While it’s been good for Mahogany to learn at her own pace, Jackson knows that when she’s older and in the workforce, that might not be an option.</p><p>“Some jobs are not doing things at your pace,” Jackson said. “They’re saying: ‘These are the timelines, this is when you need to know it by’ or ‘This is when it's done by.’ With Freestyle Learning, if you don't get it, they’re going to stay on it until you get it.”</p>

entries.title: John Summit is coming home for the holiday
entries.summary: <p>When John Summit picked up the phone on Friday the 13th, it felt like nothing short of good luck. Trying to schedule an interview with the Naperville CPA turned DJ lately has proven as difficult as getting through the endless wall of bodies at one of his festival sets.</p><p>Since releasing his sophomore album “Ctrl Escape” in April (on Tax Day, no less), Summit has been the definition of in-demand. If he wasn’t playing Red Rocks or headlining marquee festivals like Tomorrowland and Electric Daisy Carnival, he was taking over the floor of the New York Stock Exchange, launching a collaboration with toy brand Squishmallows and staging a massive, full-production arena tour (including two performances at United Center Nov. 24 and 25).</p><p>But the most significant moment of 2026 had to be his <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/lollapalooza/2026/07/30/lollapalooza-john-summit-dj-edm-naperville-headliner" >homecoming gig at Lollapalooza</a>. On July 30, Summit was one of the rare DJs to headline one of the festival’s main stages, just a day after his 32nd birthday. “That definitely the highlight so far of this year,” said Summit, born John Schuster. He chose his stage surname to symbolize reaching these new heights in his career.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-ba0000" name="module-ba0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>John Summit</h3><br><b>When:</b> 7 p.m. Nov. 24 & 8 p.m. Nov. 25<br><b>Where:</b> United Center, 1901 W. Madison<br><b>Tickets:</b> $102+<br><b>Info:</b> <a class="Link" href="https://www.ticketmaster.com/john-summit-tickets/artist/2730221" target="_blank" >ticketmaster.com</a></div> </div><p></p><div class="Figure-credit"><p><a class="Link" href="https://www.instagram.com/jamal.eid/?hl=en" target="_blank" >Jamal Eid</a></p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p> You can sense the shock and awe of that day in the professional footage archived on YouTube. For someone who spent years dealing exclusively with numbers, Summit still couldn’t compute the tens of thousands who showed up to the Bud Light Stage. “I've had many of ‘you made it’ moments in my career, but [Lollapalooza] was truly one that was a full circle one for me,” he said. </p><p>Fifteen years prior, at just 17, Summit took the Metra from Naperville to attend his first Lollapalooza. Later, he'd also regularly attended Pitchfork Music Fest, where saw indie acts like Beach House. But that time in Grant Park in 2011, standing in the crowd watching Deadmau5, changed everything for Summit — even if he didn't yet know what the future held. “It’s where I first saw and discovered electronic music and its energy. … So now it felt like a big honor to be able to give other kids their first experience and hopefully change lives like mine changed.”</p><p>Making it even more of a victory is the fact that for years, “Lollapalooza told me I couldn't play that stage," Summit revealed. "They're like, you're a DJ, you need to play Perry's Stage" where EDM acts are typically relegated during the weekend. Summit said he was offered the headlining spot at Perry’s in 2025 but he turned it down in hopes of a better placement. “And the timing worked out perfectly because now I'm doing this fall arena tour … and everyone told me I couldn't do an arena tour as a DJ, either. I love proving people wrong.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-070000" class="Figure-credit"><p>Angel Rivera</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Summit has been doing so pretty much since the beginning when he started cramming in online “how to be a DJ” tutorials while studying accounting at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign. He’d then share everything he learned with a growing fanbase on social media as a total about-face to the masked DJs he grew up with like Marshmello and Daft Punk who thrived on mystery. “I don't like the gatekeeping mentality,” Summit said. “Everyone and their mother can DJ nowadays, which is awesome, because I think the more the merrier. Plus, I have nothing to hide … and I love to give back. It's the first way I really gained fans.” Today, that community totals nearly 5 million across platforms.</p><p>After graduating college, Summit amped it up with late-night club gigs around Chicago, waking up a few hours later to begin his 9-5 at Ernst and Young. Through his regular spot at Spybar, Summit was introduced to international DJs and the influential tech house sound that was coming out of the U.K. at the time and recalled having mentors like Green Velvet and Gene Farris.</p><p>“There was a very DIY scene in Chicago that was community-driven, which was nice,” he said. “Even just the boat parties I played, there were so many ways to DJ that were outside of the system.”<b> </b></p><p>By 2019, Summit was doing so well, he was able to leave the corporate world for good to pursue music full-time and, driven by the success of hits like 2020's "Deep End," he established his own record label Experts Only and moved to the party capital of Miami.</p><p> It's all part of a journey he is finally embracing on “Ctrl Escape,” which champions rebooting your life in search of what makes you truly happy. “The thing is, I hid that part of my story for my first 10 years. I refused to tell people I went to college or that I was in a fraternity and an accountant," he said, admitting that it wasn't time wasted at least. In fact, many of the skill sets apply today, like being able to audit the finances of his label. “But I didn't want to be looked down upon because it felt like you have to be cool and have people wondering, is he from Berlin or whatever?” he joked. “Thankfully I'm from Chicago, which has legit house music roots. So I knew I had some cred.”<b> </b></p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-760000" class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>On his national arena tour, John Summit brings in lights, props, dancers, singers and multiple B stages as he angles to become the rock star of the EDM world.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p><a class="Link" href="https://www.instagram.com/jbajsel/?hl=en" target="_blank" >Julian Bajsel</a></p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>It would be remiss not to mention some of the roadblocks along the way — like his reaction to the recent Grammy snub heard round the world. When “Ctrl Escape” wasn’t nominated in any of the dance award categories announced Nov. 16, Summit <a class="Link" href="https://x.com/johnsummit/status/2122319183249551386?s=20" target="_blank" ><u>made some noise on X</u></a>, exclaiming he’s “never submitting to the Grammys again unless s--- changes.” He further called the nomination process a “f------ joke” and reduced the nominees like Madonna, Robyn and Slayyyter to “music industry fueled pop stars." Summit was quickly raked by mainstream media and even figures like Charli xcx, which had to hurt since he’s admittedly a big fan.</p><p>In our interview, Summit praised the British star’s world-building during the Brat era and said he used that model as part of the inspiration for his latest tour, where he imbues the CPA storyline into cubicle staging and his suit-and-tie attire. Fans, too, often cosplay as brokers. Other cues came from seeing artists like Tame Impala and Bad Bunny live, with Summit bringing in more lights, props, dancers, singers and multiple B stages as he angles to become the rock star of the EDM world. “I've been touring as a DJ for over 10 years. So I thought it was time to take it up a level,” he explained of the intention behind it all. While he's not the first DJ to do an arena tour, it hasn't been done quite on this production scale.</p><p>When he brings the tour home on Tuesday, though, he’s also going to find time to tone it down a notch and do normal things, like enjoying a proper Thanksgiving meal at his mom’s house and crash on the couch. “We’re not a crazy football family but now that the Bears are good, we'll probably actually watch,” he joked. “Other than that, the goal is just eating food and finally getting in a bunch of naps.”</p>

entries.title: The Army plans to detonate a toxic lead compound near the Illinois-Iowa border. Here’s what to know.
entries.summary: <p>The U.S. Army <a class="Link" href="https://www.army.mil/article/296990" target="_blank" ><u>is scheduled</u></a> to detonate a stockpile of lead azide, a chemical used for making bombs, as soon as Wednesday in Middletown, Iowa, about 80 miles southwest of the Quad Cities, pending a court challenge.</p><p>The explosion is expected to create a dust plume containing lead. Lead is toxic to humans and animals.</p><p>On Monday afternoon a federal appeals court cleared the way for the detonation. The order by the 8th Circuit U.S. Court of Appeals <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/environment/2026/11/23/trump-orders-the-army-not-to-detonate-bomb-making-chemicals-in-iowa-without-court-approval" target="_blank" >was one of two decisions</a> President Donald Trump said he was awaiting after he ordered the Army earlier in the day not to detonate the chemicals without court approval, according to the Associated Press.</p><p>Trump had weighed in on social media, saying he would defer to the courts on whether the administration should move ahead. He also said in a statement that his decision was subject to agreement by Iowa Gov.-elect Rob Sand. Though if Sand and the court don't agree, Trump said, the administration would not proceed with the detonation. He said he would hold Sand responsible. </p><p>The Army moved the planned explosion from Friday to Monday before pushing it to Wednesday after politicians from Iowa and Illinois asked for a delay and environmental groups filed a lawsuit to pause the detonation. Wednesday was chosen for optimal weather conditions, the Army said.</p><p>A Sierra Club attorney had <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/11/22/environmental-groups-say-legal-status-of-planned-lead-detonation-in-iowa-remains-uncertain" target="_blank" ><u>said on Sunday</u></a> that it was it unclear whether a court order temporarily putting on hold the Army’s EPA permit would prevent the Army from detonating the toxic material.</p><p>Here’s what else you need to know.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-990000" name="html-embed-module-990000"></a><div style="min-height:355px" id="datawrapper-vis-oMfQV"><script type="text/javascript" defer src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/oMfQV/embed.js" charset="utf-8" data-target="#datawrapper-vis-oMfQV"></script><noscript><img src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/oMfQV/full.png" alt="Locator map" /></noscript></div> </div> </div><p></p><h3><b>Why is the army detonating old munitions?</b></h3><p>There’s a risk that these stored materials will detonate on their own, and moving them could also trigger an explosion, according to the Defense Department. The issue was discovered earlier this year and plans to blow them up have been ongoing for months.</p><h3><b>When is this detonation going to happen?</b></h3><p>The detonation is expected to take place at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa on Wednesday, the Army said. The plant is around 80 miles southwest of the Quad Cities and only about 10 miles west of rural Illinois communities just across the Mississippi River.</p><p>The Army delayed the planned explosion after politicians raised concerns about safety. Both the outgoing Republican governor of Iowa and the newly elected Democratic governor called for a delay. They were joined by other politicians in both states. The environmental organization Earthjustice also sued to try to pause the detonation.</p><h3><b>Has the Army blown up lead azide before? </b></h3><p>While the Army has destroyed weapons and materials in the past, it has never blown up such a large amount of this particular chemical, according to a spokesperson.</p><p>“We detonate all the time, but we have not detonated lead azide at this quantity,” said Lori McFate, public affairs specialist with the Army Sustainment Command in Bettendorf, Iowa.</p><p>McFate said the explosion will take place after months of planning. The procedure has received a green light from the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency regional office in Kansas City. That’s a different jurisdiction than the regional EPA office in Chicago, which oversees environmental protection in Illinois.</p><h3><b>What is lead azide?</b></h3><p>Lead azide is a compound of lead and nitrogen, used to make bombs. About 5 tons of it will be blown up.</p><p>“The lead azide has aged. It's become unstable to the point where moving it or even allowing it to sit on the odd chance that it receives some sort of shock or friction could lead to a spontaneous explosion,” said Greg Domski, associate provost and professor of chemistry and biochemistry at Augustana College in Rock Island.</p><h3><b>Will the lead plume reach Chicago?</b></h3><p>The lead dust is not expected to blow as far northeast as Chicago. </p><p>Illinois <a class="Link" href="https://epa.illinois.gov/iowa-plant-updates.html" target="_blank" >has created a webpage</a> where residents can find the latest information on the situation. Current meteorological data for Wednesday, Nov. 25 on the site indicate Illinois is not expected to be affected by the detonation plume. The Illinois EPA and the Illinois Emergency Management Agency and Office of Homeland Security will continue monitoring conditions as forecasts and operational plans evolve.</p><p>Brian Pierce, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service Quad Cities forecast office said if the detonation takes place Wednesday, winds would blow the smoke into Iowa and potentially northeast Missouri.</p><p>“It would be blowing it to the southwest across the far southeast parts of Iowa,” Pierce said. “There’s a question of how high the plume would get, which we won’t know until it actually happens.”</p><h3><b>What do we know about the health effects for people?</b></h3><p>The EPA says there is no safe level of lead exposure. It is a neurotoxin that damages the central nervous system. It’s particularly harmful to children as their brains and nervous systems aren’t fully developed. Exposure to lead is associated with cognitive delays, heart problems, and reproductive issues.</p><p>“Lead is an element, and doesn't break down,” said Robert Hirschfeld, director of water policy at the Prairie River Network, a Champaign-based environmental advocacy group.</p><p>“Those health risks persist as long as the lead does.”</p><p>As part of the controlled detonation, federal officials are installing air monitors and will conduct further environmental sampling of the blast area.</p><h3><b>Will this affect crops or animals?</b></h3><p>For locations that are likely to be affected, the agricultural impacts of the lead dust are still unknown, Hirschfeld said. “We’re past harvest now, and so all of that lead is going to land on bare soil and that lead will stay there and contaminate that soil.”</p><p>He said lead contamination could go beyond the potentially impacted farmland and crops, and trickle down to animals, whether livestock or wildlife, that graze on the land.</p><h3><b>What safety precautions do people exposed to the plume need to take?</b></h3><p>The Illinois Department of Public Health <a class="Link" href="https://dph.illinois.gov/resource-center/news/2026/november/18-release-2.html" target="_blank" >recommends</a> the following safety tips:</p><ul class="rte2-style-ul" style="margin-top:0;margin-bottom:0;padding-inline-start:48px;" id="rte-4b1b1f80-e463-11f1-83d0-11b933b990fd"><li>Stay indoors and keep windows closed for 24 to 48 hours after the detonation.</li><li>If you have an HVAC system that actively draws in outside air, like a school or commercial building, then you may want to temporarily close the intake and switch to recirculate.</li><li>Use a portable air cleaner to supplement your furnace filter.</li><li>Once the U.S. Army determines the airborne exposure period has ended, wet-clean potentially affected surfaces, including playground equipment, toys, and windowsills, using soap and water. Avoid sweeping that may redistribute dust.</li><li>If you need to drive through an area impacted by dust, set your car’s AC/heater to recirculate. Afterward, you can take your car to the car wash and replace the cabin filter, if needed. A high efficiency cabin filter will capture fine particulate matter.</li><li>Wash your hands before eating and drinking and take your shoes off at the entrance when you enter your home. </li><li>Visit your doctor if you have health concerns.</li></ul><p><i>Contributing: Isabela Nieto</i></p>

uptick</b>: More than 53,000 noncitizens nationwide in 2026 have been fitted with ankle monitors under the Department of Homeland Security's Alternatives to Detention program, according to government data. That number has more than tripled since 2024 as the Trump administration has ramped up immigration enforcement.</p><p><b>Local level</b>: So far this year, ICE's Chicago field office, which oversees Illinois, Indiana, Wisconsin, Missouri, Kentucky and Kansas, has issued nearly 3,800 ankle monitors — a nearly 40% jump since 2024, our analysis found.</p><p><b>At issue</b>: The surge has raised concerns among advocates over the mental health toll they say the constant surveillance takes on those who wear the ankle device and pose no risk. Advocates argue ankle monitors were supposed to be an alternative to detention, but as more people have been fitted with them, detentions have also increased. In a statement, DHS defended the program as a critical tool.</p><p><b>Chicagoan's POV</b>: Liz, a Guatemalan asylum-seeker in Chicago, told WBEZ she has been living in a constant state of anxiety since her family was asked to show up in August for an unexpected immigration check-in. Her husband was taken into immigration custody while Liz was fitted with an ankle monitor and released with her 15-year-old daughter. Freitag</a></h5><p><b>Finding community</b>: For years, local Latino converts to Islam struggled to find religious spaces and support networks that reflected both their faith and their cultural Many have found a home in a shuttered church in Berwyn, now called Ojala Islamic Center, the Midwest's first Latino-led mosque.</p><p><b>Key context</b>: The mosque opened in February amid a shifting religious landscape. entries.title: Cubs reportedly make big pitching splash with five-year deal for free-agent lefty Trevor Rogers
entries.summary: <p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a> signaled they were going to spend their energy and resources focusing on pitching this offseason, and they’ve reportedly delivered on that front in a big way before Thanksgiving.</p><p>According to multiple reports, the team has agreed to a five-year contract with free-agent pitcher Trevor Rogers worth $120 million.</p><p>Rogers, a 29-year-old left-hander, was a first-round pick of the Marlins in 2017 and had a stellar rookie season in 2021, finishing runner-up in the NL Rookie of the Year vote. He never replicated that statistical greatness – a 2.64 ERA in 25 starts – with Miami and was dealt to the Orioles in a deadline deal in 2024.</p><p>Those gaudy numbers returned a year later, and back from the minor leagues, he had a spectacular 1.81 ERA in 18 starts in 2025. Last season, he made 30 starts, finishing the season with a 4.03 ERA. He was particularly good from June on, posting a 2.90 ERA in his final 20 starts to set himself up as one of the top starting pitchers in this offseason’s free-agent class, considered, perhaps, the No. 2 arm on the market after two-time Cy Young winner Tarik Skubal, the winter’s top prize who landed a record-setting $450 million contract from the Mets.</p><p>The Cubs actually got an up-close look at Rogers last season, when the southpaw held the game’s top-scoring offense to one run in six innings in early July.</p><p>Now, he’ll be doing his dealing for the Cubs, and it’s a big addition for a team that entered the offseason in desperate need of pitching improvements.</p><p>All five of the pitchers who finished last season in the North Side rotation left for free agency, and the stable of in-house candidates to fill those vacancies bring along big question marks, with the likes of Justin Steele, Ben Brown and Cade Horton all coming off significant injuries.</p><p>Rogers provides some much needed stability on that front and figures to top the team starting staff whenever the season begins after what’s anticipated to be a lengthy lockout. But even if the 2027 season is significantly impacted by a work stoppage, this is a clear long-term move, with Rogers reportedly locked up for a half decade.</p><p>Jed Hoyer’s front office doesn’t figure to be done adding on the pitching front, and it wouldn’t surprise to see more work completed in short order, with the aforementioned lockout expected to freeze the sport – and offseason activity with it – at the start of next month.</p>

entries.title: Man killed, woman wounded in stabbing inside Lower West Side apartment building
entries.summary: <p>A 78-year-old woman and 86-year-old man were stabbed in a Lower West Side apartment building Monday evening, police said. </p><p>Around 7:59 p.m., a 44-year-old man who lived in the building went upstairs to the victims' apartment in the 2100 block of West 19th Street to confront them, according to police. A fight broke out and the offender stabbed the older couple multiple times with a sharp object before fleeing.</p><p>The woman suffered multiple stab wounds to her torso and was taken to Stroger Hospital, where she was listed in fair condition.</p><p>The man suffered multiple stab wounds to his upper body and was taken to Mount Sinai Hospital, where he was pronounced dead.</p><p>Police say the 44-year-old man was arrested near the scene and charges are pending. Area Three detectives are investigating.</p>

entries.title: Before Salem Named Tituba a Witch, She Had a World. Theater Director Charlotte Brathwaite Reimagines It
entries.summary: <p>For director Charlotte Brathwaite, theater is a place where the past comes into conversation with the present.</p><p>She moves freely across genres to create immersive performances that bring together music, ritual and movement, inviting audiences to encounter histories that continue to shape our lives.</p><p>“I’m interested in what remains when the official record is incomplete: The things carried through music, movement, memory, language and the body,” said Brathwaite, winner of the 2023 Doris Duke Artist Award who, at 16, found her theatrical home at La MaMa Experimental Theatre Club in New York and who teaches at the New School in Greenwich Village.</p><p>That’s the backstory to Brathwaite’s role as director of Court Theatre’s “Tituba,” the story of an enslaved woman accused in the Salem, Massachusetts witch trials of 1692 and featured in playwright Arthur Miller’s classic, “The Crucible.”</p><p>Court Theatre presents “Tituba” Dec. 10-20 at the University of Chicago’s Rockefeller Memorial Chapel, 5850 S. Woodlawn Ave.</p><p>“I'm interested in the idea that, through theater, the dead return because there’s unfinished business,” Brathwaite said. “When we bring these stories back to life, we’re not simply revisiting the past. We’re confronting histories that are still with us, questions that remain unresolved, and people whose voices still have something to teach us about the present.”</p><p>“For me, that's the power of theater,” Brathwaite said. “We gather in a room, unmediated, sharing the same air and experiencing something together. There’s power in numbers, in the act of gathering itself. A story from hundreds of years ago can suddenly become urgent, alive, and deeply connected to the world we're living in now.”</p><p>“I work across theater, film, dance and installation because I’m interested in what happens when these forms meet,” she said. “Each brings a different language, and together they allow me to create experiences that can’t necessarily exist within one form alone.”</p><p>That’s because, as Brathwaite puts it, “History isn't something that sits safely behind us. It continues to shape our relationships, our institutions, our ideas about who belongs, who is believed, and whose humanity is recognized.”</p><p>Tituba, the two-part theatrical event, starts with an original ritual oratorio Brathwaite conceived and wrote, with music by esperanza spalding and two choirs.</p><p>The choirs comprise a core choir — Uniting Voices Chicago, formerly known as the Chicago Children’s Choir — and community choir The Vocal Shed, founded by Chicago-based singer and songwriter Alysha Monique, which serves as an experiential laboratory for vocalists of all skill levels.</p><p>The work draws inspiration from the world imagined in Maryse Condé's novel “I, Tituba, Black Witch of Salem<i>”</i> alongside actual testimony from the Salem witch trials.</p><p>The second part is Winsome Pinnock’s solo play, performed by award-winning actress Sydney Charles, a native of Chicago’s own Far Southeast Side.</p><p>Pinnock’s play gives Tituba the space to tell her own story, confronting the accusations, violence and systems of power that sought to define her.</p><p>The two works are in conversation with one another. The oratorio begins before Salem, before the accusations, before Tituba became known to history as a witch.</p><p>“I'm interested in imagining the world she came from, the people who loved her, the knowledge she carried, and the community that existed before her life was defined by violence and accusation,” Brathwaite said.</p><p>Tituba’s connection to Barbados also resonated with Brathwaite, whose parents are both from the island.</p><p>“This is someone I want[ed] to know more about,” she said.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> </div><p>It’s the latest in Brathwaite’s Chicago portfolio, which includes directing Tamar-kali’s “Demon Fruit Blues” at the Museum of Contemporary Art Chicago eight years ago.</p><p>Her inventiveness continues to keep her calendar full.</p><p>Brathwaite also is developing “Douglass: The Reckoning” with journalist June Cross. As part of that process, the directors held public Town Halls at La MaMa and 651 ARTS in New York on Nov. 2 and Nov. 9, inviting audiences into the questions shaping the work.</p><p>In May 2027, she directs Eisa Davis’ “Angela's Mixtape” at Signature Theatre in New York. It’s a personal exploration of family, identity and political inheritance, shaped in part by Davis’s relationship with her aunt, the activist Angela Davis.</p><p>Separately, Brathwaite and Senegalese visual artist Malick Welli are building Malidoma Popenguine, an artist residency and cultural space. The project grew from their ongoing collaboration, “Forgotten Paradise,” and a shared interest in art, land, memory and community. It’s in the village of Popenguine-Ndayane, a commune about 43 miles, or 70 kilometers, southeast of Dakar.</p><p>Brathwaite said the project is deeply connected to her early experiences at La MaMa, where the now-late Ellen Stewart, founder of La MaMa Experimental Theatre Club, created a home for artists from around the world.</p><p>“I experienced firsthand what it means for an artist to have a place to experiment, take risks, and develop work within a community,” Brathwaite said. “That experience continues to shape how I think about making spaces for others.”</p><p>Brathwaite sees a connection between the spaces she creates for artists and communities and the world she’s building around Tituba.</p><p>“I’m interested in what happens when we bring people together, not simply to watch art, but to participate in something,” she said.</p><p>“For me, gathering is part of the work. It’s about creating a space where we can listen to one another, question what we’ve inherited, and consider whose stories have been left out, who belongs, and who gets to be heard.”</p>

entries.title: Cubs keep spending in free agency, reportedly land Japanese slugger Teruaki Sato on six-year deal
entries.summary: <p>After a reported big-money deal for a pitcher to top their starting rotation, the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a> have reportedly made another high-priced bet on a bat.</p><p>The free-agent dollars apparently kept flowing, with the Cubs following <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/11/24/cubs-trevor-rogers-mlb-offseason-free-agents-rumors-pitching-starting-rotation-2027" >a five-year, $120 million contract for lefty arm Trevor Rogers</a> with another big splash, a six-year, $120 million pact with Japanese slugger Teruaki Sato, according to multiple reports.</p><p>The 27-year-old is a two-time MVP of Japan’s Central League, spending the last six seasons with the Hanshin Tigers. He won that league’s Triple Crown in 2026, with a huge season that saw the lefty batsman hit .306 with a .383 on-base percentage to go along with 39 homers and 106 RBIs.</p><p>Sato mostly played third base in Japan, though he played some outfield, and according to ESPN’s Jeff Passan, he will be dropped into one of the Cubs’ two vacant corner-outfield spots, with Gold Glove winner Alex Bregman manning the hot corner. It stands to reason the designated-hitter spot could be an option for Craig Counsell as he plots his lineups, as well.</p><p>Sato arrives on the North Side as his countryman, Seiya Suzuki, appears primed to depart. Suzuki played five years with the Cubs after a career in Japan and put up strong offensive numbers, earning him the status as perhaps the top free-agent hitter this offseason.</p><p>The Cubs extended a qualifying offer to Suzuki, though <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/11/17/cubs-seiya-suzuki-qualifying-offer-free-agent-mlb-offseason-rumors-right-field" >that was rejected</a>, assuring the team will receive a draft pick should he sign elsewhere, an outcome that wouldn’t surprise should bidding for Suzuki escalate.</p><p>In the outfield, longtime left fielder Ian Happ is also a free agent. The Cubs have 2026 reserves Matt Shaw and Pedro Ramirez and spent the GM meetings talking about that duo’s potential to take over corner-outfield duties, despite their histories as infielders. At least one, perhaps, won’t have to be relied on to assume such a role with Sato now in the fold.</p><p>It obviously remains to be seen whether Sato’s offensive success in Japan will translate to the major leagues. The Cubs have had success turning Suzuki and lefty pitcher Shota Imanaga into key pieces in the U.S., and they could certainly use the offensive oomph with Suzuki potentially departing, even after the lineup scored more runs than any team during the 2026 regular season.</p><p>While Jed Hoyer’s front office forecasted an offseason focused on pitching improvements — like the addition of Rogers — it has plenty else to do, particularly with a third of the starting lineup off to free agency. Sato does a good deal to fill the gap in that department.</p><p>Though fans have been frustrated the big-market Cubs haven’t spent a gargantuan amount of free-agent dollars — seemingly never intent on launching into the bidding war for top-of-the-market arm Tarik Skubal, who netted a record-setting $450 million contract from the Mets — Hoyer & Co. have spent big in free agency for a second straight winter. Bregman received a $175 million contract last offseason, and now just two players have accounted for $240 million with much work still to do.</p>
entries.author: Vinnie Duber

entries.title: Man killed in Humboldt Park shooting
entries.summary: <p>A 43-year-old man was shot and killed in Humboldt Park late Monday night, police said. </p><p>The shooting occurred at the 3300 block of W. Evergreen Ave at around 9:05 p.m, according to police. The victim sustained a gunshot wound to his chest and officers attempted CPR on the scene before transporting him to Mt. Sinai Hospital. He was later pronounced dead. </p><p>No suspect has been arrested or identified. Area Five detectives are investigating the incident. </p>

entries.title: Amtrak scraps controversial Bridgeport plan that would have cleared path for Sox to build new stadium
entries.summary: <p>Plans that would have allowed Amtrak to move a controversial maintenance facility to Bridgeport have come to a screeching halt after the Federal Railroad Administration on Monday pulled funding and called the plan “fiscally untenable.”</p><p>An Amtrak spokesman said the rail agency “is shifting its focus to redevelopment of our existing 14th Street Yard as a better long-term approach to modernizing our Chicago maintenance facilities.”</p><p>“The redevelopment of Amtrak’s existing Chicago Coach Yard at 14th Street, which offers better operational access to Chicago Union Station, will provide substantial benefits to the traveling public,” Amtrak spokesman Marc Magliari said in an email. “Amtrak will focus on addressing critical infrastructure needs, improved support for new trains and helping to advance future Midwest service growth.”</p><p>Amtrak had planned to sell its 14th Street property to move to the existing Canal Street rail yard in Bridgeport, which drew massive community opposition. White Sox minority owner <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2025/06/06/justin-ishbia-white-sox-jerry-reinsdorf-ownership-winnetka" target="_blank" ><u>Justin Ishbia’s</u></a> company, Canal Edge LLC, had proposed a mixed-use development called <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/09/05/new-sox-park-future-owner-announces-proposal-for-riverside-stadium-at-the-railyards" target="_blank" ><u>the Railyards as the site for a new White Sox stadium</u></a>, which would have been built where an Amtrak railyard now operates.</p><p>Trains.com first reported the FRA funding decision, citing a letter to interim Amtrak President Byl Herrmann from FRA Administrator David Fink on Monday. </p><p>“Subsequent due diligence by Amtrak and Canal Edge LLC has exposed major, previously unquantified infrastructure costs that render the Canal Street relocation fiscally untenable. Most notably, an independent life cycle analysis estimates approximately $400 million in cumulative costs over 50 years, above and beyond the work to be funded by the grant, to stabilize 17 viaducts and bridges at the site,” Fink wrote in the letter.</p><p>Ald. Nicole Lee (11th), who lives near the proposed development and led the political charge against it, applauded federal officials for tanking the plan.</p><p>“As we have always said, this site, situated squarely amid a residential area, was not a feasible location for this maintenance facility,” Lee said in a statement. “We have advocated relentlessly to ensure this project did not destroy the neighborhood that thousands of Chicagoans call home, and we are proud to have succeeded.”</p><p>“We continue to support investment in our rail networks, and look forward to a conversation about upgrading the viaducts in the 11th Ward and other such infrastructure across the region,” Lee said. “We also look forward to a discussion about the future of the White Sox and a path to reimagining 35th Street to be a more vibrant economic environment surrounding our team. That work must start today.”</p><p>Lee also thanked “the thousands of residents who organized, raised money for legal support, wrote letters to the editor, signed petitions, showed up for community and County Board and City Council meetings, and more. You stood up strongly for our environment, for public health, and for our community’s future.”</p><p>A spokesperson for Ishbia did not immediately provide a comment. </p><p>Work had been expected to start as early as this fall, after Amtrak announced it had secured the federal funding in August, portending a lucrative game of musical chairs between the South Loop and Bridgeport. </p><p>Ishbia planned to pump more than $125 million into Canal Edge LLC, the entity financing and delivering the new $900 million Amtrak facility in Bridgeport. </p><p>That would’ve opened up 47 acres on the west bank of the Chicago River south of Roosevelt Road for Ishbia to build a stadium. His firm released gleaming <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/09/05/new-sox-park-future-owner-announces-proposal-for-riverside-stadium-at-the-railyards" target="_blank" ><u>renderings</u></a> of an open-air park with sweeping skyline views. </p><p>But the land swap faced overwhelming neighborhood opposition from residents of Armour Square and Bridgeport who were stunned to learn a 24/7 rail maintenance facility would be thrust into the residential area. </p><p>The Sox announced<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2025/06/05/white-sox-jerry-reinsdorf-justin-ishbia-ownership-transfer-new-stadium" target="_blank" > <u>a potential succession plan last year</u></a> potentially giving Ishbia the option to buy a controlling interest in the Sox from chairman Jerry Reinsdorf as early as 2029. </p><p>Reinsdorf previously tried and failed to lobby state lawmakers to help fund a new stadium across the river from the site eyed by Ishbia, the so-called 78 (for Chicago’s 78th community area) where billionaire Chicago Fire owner Joe Mansueto is building a soccer stadium. </p><p>The scrapped railyard plan likely also throws a wrench in developers’ proposal for the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears-stadium/2026/10/28/bridgeport-bears-domed-stadium-proposal-sox-rate-field" target="_blank" ><u>Chicago Bears to build a stadium where Rate Field now stands</u></a> and where the Sox are under lease through 2029.</p><p>That idea was already a long shot among several city-based proposals for the Bears that developers have floated in recent weeks without participation from the team or Mayor Brandon Johnson.</p><p>The Bears, who have insisted their Illinois focus is on Arlington Heights while they consider sites in Hammond, Indiana, are hoping state lawmakers pass municipal stadium authority legislation <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears-stadium/2026/11/16/bears-stadium-bill-illinois-lawmakers-fall-veto-session-house-speaker-replacement-data-centers?5" target="_blank" ><u>next week</u></a> to help build a publicly owned dome.</p>

entries.title: Woman charged in August shooting that left 1 dead, 2 injured
entries.summary: <p>A woman is facing first-degree murder charges in an August shooting that killed a man and injured two others in Bronzeville on the South Side. </p><p>Tatianna Hill, 27, is accused of shooting from a crowd that was gathered in the 100 block of East 37th Street on Aug. 29 and hitting three people, Chicago Police said. </p><p>Antonio Hollis, 32, suffered multiple gunshot wounds and was pronounced dead, police said. </p><p>A 31-year-old man was also in critical condition, police said. A 23-year-old woman, shot in her hand, was in good condition.</p><p>Hill was arrested Monday and charged with one count of first-degree murder, two counts of attempted first-degree murder and two counts of aggravated battery. </p><p>She was expected to appear in court Tuesday. </p>

entries.title: Cinco personas, incluyendo 3 bomberos, resultan heridas durante un incendio en Back of the Yards
entries.summary: <p>Tres bomberos se encuentran entre cinco personas heridas durante un incendio que arrasó un edificio en el vecindario de Back of the Yards la tarde del lunes.</p><p>El incendio se desató alrededor de las 12:20 p.m. en la cuadra 4800 al sur de Damen Avenue, según un portavoz del Departamento de Bomberos, y fue extinguido a las 2:10 p.m.</p><p>Tres bomberos y dos civiles fueron llevados a hospitales, según el portavoz. entries.title: Bears predictions: Week 12 at Lions
entries.summary: <p>The Sun-Times' <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> experts make their picks for the Thanksgiving game against the Lions at Ford Field:</p><h3><b>Patrick Finley</b></h3><h3></h3><p><b>Bears, 30-27: </b>The Bears stop a string of Ford Field horrors. In 2023, they gave up 17 points in the last 3 minutes to lose; in 2024, Matt Eberflus forgot to use his timeout; and in 2025, they were humiliated by 31. <b>Season</b>: 5-5.</p><h3><b>Jason Lieser</b></h3><p><b>Bears, 34-31:</b> The Lions have had concerns defensively throughout the last few seasons, and Ben Johnson finally will exploit them. <b>Season:</b> 6-4.</p><h3><b>Scoop Jackson</b></h3><p><b>Bears 21, Lions 21 (tie): </b>ESPN left open a 0.4% chance this game ends in a tie (45.1% Bears win, 54.5% Lions win). I predicted as much at the beginning of the season. This has all of the makings to make me genius. Or a fool. <b>Season</b>: 6-4.</p><h3><b>Steve Greenberg</b></h3><p><b>Lions, 27-23:</b> New rule: Until the Bears actually win a division game, I'm not picking them in one. The Lions are functioning at a much higher level than the Bears offensively — and don't look now, but their defense is pretty good. <b>Season</b>: 7-3.</p><h3><b>Jeff Agrest</b></h3><p><b>Lions, 31-24:</b> The Bears and Lions have played mostly nondescript games against each other since 1930. But this won’t be one of them. Remarkably, it’s the biggest game in the history of the NFL’s second-longest rivalry. The Lions’ offense will carry the day. <b>Season</b>: 5-5.<br></p>
entries.author: Jason Lieser

entries.title: Druski to host Chicago's New Year's Eve celebration from Navy Pier
entries.summary: <p>Award-winning comedian and actor Druski will host Chicago’s celebration during ABC’s Dick Clark’s New Year’s Rockin’ Eve broadcast. The first round of free tickets will be available at 10 a.m. Wednesday, according to the city’s Department of Cultural Affairs and Special Events.</p><p>Druski is a popular internet personality and comedian whose recent appearance as host of NBC's legendary sketch comedy show “Saturday Night Live” was the most watched episode in the last two years. The Georgia native also hosted the BET Awards this summer, becoming the youngest host of the show's history at 31.</p><p>The city says this year’s New Year’s Eve celebration will take place at Navy Pier with a live countdown at midnight central time and fireworks. The party will be televised on ABC starting at 7 p.m. on Dec. 31.</p><p>The event will also feature a slate of Chicago musicians, including Grammy-nominated producer and songwriter Steve “Silk” Hurley. The city said a Grammy-winning headliner will be announced soon.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" entries.title: Man in critical condition from Roseland fire
entries.summary: <p>A fire broke out in Roseland early Wednesday, according to police.</p><p>Around 4:15 a.m., a man was found unresponsive in the burning building at the 0-100 block of East 103rd Street, police said. entries.title: Café de noroeste de Chicago, Tasa Coffee Roasters, es acusado de vínculos con ICE
entries.summary: <p>Algunos miembros de la comunidad están pidiendo un boicot a una cafetería popular en West Humboldt Park, y trabajadores abandonaron sus puestos tras una publicación viral en redes sociales que alega que la tienda tiene vínculos con ICE.</p><p>El lunes, además, le arrojaron huevos.</p><p>Jackie Márquez es la propietaria de <a class="Link" href="https://www.tasa.coffee/" target="_blank" >Tasa Coffee Roasters</a>, una tostadora y cafetería ubicada en 4136 W. North Ave. La tienda abrió en 2022 y rápidamente se convirtió en una favorita del vecindario por su enfoque “de propiedad y con perspectiva latina”.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-dc0000" name="module-dc0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>Pero una publicación que comenzó a circular en redes sociales la mañana del lunes afirma que alguien con el mismo nombre que un hombre vinculado a la cafetería aparece en una base de datos del Departamento de Seguridad Nacional (DHS) que fue expuesto a finales de octubre.</p><p>WBEZ/Sun-Times puede confirmar que los documentos filtrados listan a esa persona como exoficial de supervisión de detención y deportación en la agencia. Registros públicos revisados por WBEZ/Sun-Times indican que un individuo con ese nombre ha sido empleado por DHS, pero la agencia no ofreció una confirmación directa sobre su estatus o puesto.</p><p>No se ha podido confirmar si el hombre mencionado en la filtración es en verdad la misma persona identificada en la publicación viral, y por ello no lo publicamos.</p><p>Una búsqueda en la base de datos de registros públicos Nexis mostró una dirección de correo electrónico de ICE y una ubicación de empleo de DHS asociadas al nombre del hombre en cuestión. Pero WBEZ/Sun-Times no pudo confirmar de forma independiente que el hombre sea, o haya sido, empleado de ICE.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Restos de yema y cáscara de huevo cubren la acera después de que arrojaron huevos contra la ventana de Tasa Coffee Roasters, 4136 W. North Ave., el lunes. La cafetería de Humboldt Park ha sido el blanco de rumores que intentan vincularla con la agencia de Inmigración y Control de Aduanas (ICE).</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>La licencia comercial y las subvenciones de la tienda disponibles públicamente están todas únicamente a nombre de Jackie Márquez. Los registros públicos vinculan a la pareja mediante documentos de hipoteca y de matrimonio.</p><p>El lunes por la tarde, algunos vecinos se juntaron frente a la tienda para ver los carteles que dejaron los trabajadores y que decían, “Tras enterarnos a través de Reddit de que existen acusaciones al respecto, nosotros —los baristas y tostadores de café— hemos cerrado por el día de hoy. No respaldamos, toleramos, apoyamos ni aceptamos a ninguna persona u organización vinculada a ICE. Como baristas, estamos deliberando sobre qué medidas debemos tomar. Nuestra intención, como empleados, es actuar con la mayor honestidad y transparencia posibles. Gracias”.</p><p>Para las 4 p.m. del lunes, la propia Márquez había publicado una historia de Instagram que abordaba brevemente la situación: “Soy Jackie, la única propietaria de Tasa Coffee Roasters. Soy chef. La gastronomía y el café han sido mi única trayectoria profesional. Personalmente, no estoy de acuerdo con la política migratoria actual; creo en el diálogo civil y en el respeto mutuo, incluso cuando existen diferencias de opinión. Pido que mis empleados no sean blanco de ataques ni se les responsabilice por cuestiones que están fuera de su control. Mi compromiso sigue firme con mis empleados, mis clientes y mi comunidad”.</p><p>Ni Márquez ni el hombre al que señalan habían respondido a una solicitud de comentario el lunes por la noche.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-a10083" name="image-a10083"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/5e3ad74/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fc3%2F1f%2F7ed48a874ea99940c0b6838b9585%2Fnewtasa-261124-11.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/3c32812/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fc3%2F1f%2F7ed48a874ea99940c0b6838b9585%2Fnewtasa-261124-11.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/7a18a12/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fc3%2F1f%2F7ed48a874ea99940c0b6838b9585%2Fnewtasa-261124-11.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Tasa Coffee Roasters, 4136 W. North Ave., en Humboldt Park, el lunes 23 de noviembre de 2026." srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/7a18a12/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fc3%2F1f%2F7ed48a874ea99940c0b6838b9585%2Fnewtasa-261124-11.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/6ccfb30/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fc3%2F1f%2F7ed48a874ea99940c0b6838b9585%2Fnewtasa-261124-11.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/7a18a12/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fc3%2F1f%2F7ed48a874ea99940c0b6838b9585%2Fnewtasa-261124-11.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Tasa Coffee Roasters, 4136 W. North Ave., ha sido el blanco de rumores en redes sociales, y el lunes los empleados abandonaron sus puestos en señal de protesta.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Esme Segura, de 28 años, se enteró de las acusaciones contra Tasa y decidió ir a ver con una amiga.</p><p>Llegaron con la intención de tomar fotos y videos de los carteles que habían colocado los trabajadores. Pero cuando comenzaron a grabar un video de la tienda cerrada, un hombre en el interior empezó a arrancar los carteles e hizo un gesto indicando una pequeña pistola en la cintura. WBEZ/Sun-Times revisó el video.</p><p>“Empezó a golpear la puerta y a hacernos gestos obscenos. Luego también sacó o mostró una pistola que llevaba en la cintura; se subió la camisa y dejó ver que la tenía”, dijo Segura.</p><p>La policía fue llamada al lugar y el hombre fue detenido temporalmente. Nadie en la escena quiso presentar una denuncia, por lo que la policía lo liberó tras confirmar que posee permiso legal para portar un arma de fuego, dijeron los oficiales presentes. No se ha confirmado la identidad del hombre.</p><p>Dado que Chicago ha sido un blanco habitual de las acciones federales de inmigración, dijo Segura, a la comunidad le importa si existen vínculos con la agencia que realiza detenciones y deportaciones.</p><p><i>Contribuyó: Cam Rodríguez </i></p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (IA) y editado por los seres humanos de</i> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a><br></p>

entries.title: Review: Stella Lefty took the ‘long way home’ to Lincoln Hall
entries.summary: <p>To no one’s surprise, Stella Lefty drew a packed house at Lincoln Hall on Monday.</p><p>The sold-out gig was an anticipated hometown show “about an hour” south of where she grew up in north suburban Glencoe, she told the crowd, and marked the finale of her current small club tour before she resets for bigger turf next year, including the Aragon in February. The concert also came as Lefty’s uber hit “Boston” is still sitting at No. 2 on the Billboard Hot 100 chart, 33 weeks after it debuted, even as the Noah Kahan plagiarism conversation has persisted.</p><p>Lefty is one of the biggest rising stars of the moment but also one of the most vilified —and her packed yet mediocre Lincoln Hall show didn’t do much to shift the balance to either side.</p><p>The 24-year-old, born Stella Lefkofsky, brought in reinforcements for the night to make her case. Her boyfriend, fellow up-and-coming country artist Vincent Mason (the one with the “blue eyes” she sings about) dropped by to provide umph on the couple’s duet “Something to Lose,” just days after they appeared together at the CMA Awards.</p><p>Tourmate and best friend/songwriting partner Grace Enger also crashed the stage for a sit-down cover of Taylor Swift’s “Fifteen” that the two practiced just 10 minutes before the show began. “We hope we did Taylor justice. That’s all we live for,” Lefty declared, which only added to her reputation as a frequent imitator. The comment felt even messier on the same day Vanity Fair<i> </i>dropped a hit piece about the megastar.</p><p>But duets and covers (also including a take on Natasha Bedingfield’s “Unwritten”) were the best of what Lefty had to offer in the hourlong set. The 14 other songs, Lefty originals, were unmemorable filler, victims of pattern-heavy <i>self-</i>plagiarism and full of country music cliches, delivered with a voice that has a nice rasp but lacks power moves.</p><p> The only things we truly learned about Lefty after Monday’s set is she loves to make out (“Lean In, Kiss Me” followed by yet another “Kiss Me”), loves to drink (“Whiskey” and the lineup of wine and spirits she references on “I Know I Know”) and has a history of breakups (“Good at Leaving” and a brand-new unreleased song called “Lookin’ Like Leaving”). “A lot of my songs are love songs,” she said Monday. Which would be fine except that her catalog often feels like country role play, conveniently scooting in at a time that women are dominating the genre. Not helping is the odd Southern drawl heard on some tracks that isn’t fooling anyone who knows full well she went to New Trier High School. </p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-a50000" name="image-a50000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/e87eda2/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3000x1684+0+158/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fcc%2F03%2F96ab53be419189a833c5f0552efb%2Fstellalefty-261125-19.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/d0221d7/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3000x1684+0+158/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fcc%2F03%2F96ab53be419189a833c5f0552efb%2Fstellalefty-261125-19.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/dbffbb8/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3000x1684+0+158/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fcc%2F03%2F96ab53be419189a833c5f0552efb%2Fstellalefty-261125-19.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Stella Lefty performs at Lincoln Hall, Monday, Nov. 23, 2026. " srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/dbffbb8/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3000x1684+0+158/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fcc%2F03%2F96ab53be419189a833c5f0552efb%2Fstellalefty-261125-19.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/10ea8f3/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3000x1684+0+158/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fcc%2F03%2F96ab53be419189a833c5f0552efb%2Fstellalefty-261125-19.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/dbffbb8/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3000x1684+0+158/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fcc%2F03%2F96ab53be419189a833c5f0552efb%2Fstellalefty-261125-19.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Stella Lefty performs Monday at Lincoln Hall. Lefty, born Stella Lefkofsky, remains one of the biggest rising stars of the moment but also one of the most vilified.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Tyler Pasciak LaRiviere/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Lefty has been dodging the authenticity claims for a while now, at first driven by her family ties. Her billionaire dad is Groupon co-founder Eric Lefkofsky, who is founder and CEO of health technology and artificial intelligence firm Tempus AI. He proudly watched Monday’s show from the balcony with other family members like any good dad would do.</p><p>Even if many have tried to use this affluent background as proof of Lefty’s “nepo baby” or “industry plant” status, that’s not what this is. In Lefty’s case, it’s simply privilege that has rubbed many the wrong way, especially when you consider the working-class roots of her chosen genre. Lefty likely didn’t have to work dead-end jobs to fuel her career or tough choices between taking gigs or paying her bills. She didn’t even initially have plans to be an artist, but after posting snippets to TikTok and watching the algorithm do its thing, offers came in and she was rushed into the spotlight before being properly developed or finding her own lane. You can’t fully blame Lefty for all the fallout, as culpability also falls on the lazy A&R practice nowadays of scouting social media for popularity and thinking that makes an instant star. </p><p>But in recent months, the conversation around Lefty’s legitimacy has taken on a more serious tone after claims of pilfered material arose around her debut album “Long Way Home,” released in August on Atlantic Outpost, shortly after her Lollapalooza debut.</p><p>As she ended her Lincoln Hall set with “Boston,” there was no denying the very similar melody of Noah Kahan’s “Stick Season” (while Lefty has said she wasn’t thinking of Kahan when she wrote it, she wound up giving him a co-writing credit). Fans at Lincoln Hall sang it with her anyway, including the large number of kids in the crowd.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-1b0000" name="image-1b0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/41fecb0/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3000x1684+0+158/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F5e%2F29%2F0a52d1324ab388af62498e9e6a64%2Fstellalefty-261125-24.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/d30f11f/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3000x1684+0+158/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F5e%2F29%2F0a52d1324ab388af62498e9e6a64%2Fstellalefty-261125-24.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/1231e79/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3000x1684+0+158/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F5e%2F29%2F0a52d1324ab388af62498e9e6a64%2Fstellalefty-261125-24.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Stella Lefty performs at Lincoln Hall, Monday, Nov. 23, 2026. " srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/1231e79/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3000x1684+0+158/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F5e%2F29%2F0a52d1324ab388af62498e9e6a64%2Fstellalefty-261125-24.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/4640a8c/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3000x1684+0+158/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F5e%2F29%2F0a52d1324ab388af62498e9e6a64%2Fstellalefty-261125-24.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/1231e79/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3000x1684+0+158/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F5e%2F29%2F0a52d1324ab388af62498e9e6a64%2Fstellalefty-261125-24.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Stella Lefty performs Monday at Lincoln Hall.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Tyler Pasciak LaRiviere/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Lefty has also borrowed from The Chicks’ “There’s Your Trouble” for her track “Summer You Were Mine;” it was apparently an approved grab, but still, the songwriters Tia Sillers and Mark Selby were initially left off the credits. Others have heard Blake Shelton in “Why Wouldn’t We” and even Wheatus in “Seven Eleven.” The allegations have gotten so bad, Lefty was spoofed on a recent episode of “Saturday Night Live,” which she didn’t rebut but simply called “funny asf” in a repost to her Instagram Stories.</p><p>She came off similarly unaffected Monday. Dressed in jeans and a T-shirt, Lefty had a laid-back vibe and was clearly focused on the future. “I’m very excited to be here with you guys. And I’m coming back many more times,” she foreshadowed, before giving a nod to her hometown and the Bears.</p><p>And the truth is, she probably will. While industry accolades continue to elude her, like coming up empty during the recent Grammy nominations, Lefty is doing just fine. “Boston” probably isn’t leaving the charts anytime soon. Next year’s tour is largely sold out and she’s also playing the famed country venue Ryman Auditorium in Nashville and opening up for Morgan Wallen on his tour next year. Windy City Smokeout is on the agenda, too. In September, she even replaced her original management and publicity team as she seemingly tries to change the narrative. But the question remains: What will that story be and will anyone take her seriously when she figures it out?</p><h3>Stella Lefty set list for Nov. 23, 2026 show at Lincoln Hall</h3><p>Lean In, Kiss Me<br>Why Wouldn't We<br>Thinking ’bout You<br>Good At Leaving<br>Summer You Were Mine<br>Lookin' Like Leaving<br>Kiss Me<br>Cynic<br>Could’ve Been Me<br>Fifteen (Taylor Swift cover, with Grace Enger)<br>My Kinda Love (song with Bailey Zimmerman)<br>Something to Lose (with Vincent Mason)<br>Whiskey<br>Unwritten (Natasha Bedingfield cover)<br>I Know I Know<br>Slow Dancin'<br>Boston</p>
