entries.title: Miguel Vargas more focused on improving defense than a long-term contract with White Sox
entries.summary: <p>In the second half of 2026, interviews with <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" >White Sox</a> hitting coaches about what key hitters in the lineup were working on would stall when the conversation arrived at Miguel Vargas.</p><p>What, they asked in return, could be of concern with Vargas? While he was human and imperfect like any other hitter, Vargas repeatedly demonstrated the ability to self-correct. Vargas was good, he would be fine. Or as Sox hitting coach Derek Shomon once termed it: “Vargy is a dog.”</p><p>Even amid his nightmarish 2024 season, Vargas has always demonstrated the patience of Job at the plate, and above-average skill for making contact. What he used to lack was power.</p><p>“Chris [Getz] was very straightforward,” hitting director Ryan Fuller told the Sun-Times in September. “‘Vargy, you’ve got to take care of your body. You’ve got to get stronger. We see a whole other level for you, but you’ve got to go after it.’ To his credit, you look at the 2024 season — bat speed, average exit velocity, his OPS — just the type of performer he was from 2024 to ‘25, and now ‘26, it's just been a really nice progression.”</p><p>Now that Vargas has ripped off a season where he hit .250/.363/.474, made an All-Star team and finished sixth in American League MVP voting with 33 home runs worth of demonstrated power, he’s internally viewed as a strong offensive contributor for years to come.</p><p>"It means a lot, especially after all I came through since I've been with the White Sox; not just for me but for the whole organization,” Vargas said on Tuesday. “It proved that I'm an All-Star and to help my team go to the postseason, it means a lot for me. I know what it means for the city.”</p><p>Vargas is arbitration-eligible for the first time this season and under team control through 2029, so his contract status is no urgent matter; least of all for a White Sox front office that’s working on landing another starting pitching target before a lockout begins on Dec. 1. And while his central place on the ballclub is the sort of thing that’s often affirmed with a long-term contract, the 27-year-old would just as soon focus on other things.</p><p>“Contracts or anything like that, I don't want it to be a distraction for me,” said Vargas, who indicated he has not talked extension with the Sox. “ I'm very excited for what is coming for me and my future on the South Side. Hopefully I can stay there for many more years."</p><p>Assuming he does, Vargas’ long-term fit with his close friend fellow extension candidate Munetaka Murakami might need some smoothing to maintain. Defensive metrics rate Vargas as below-average at third base, and much better at first, but he views improvement with the glove as his next developmental mountain to climb.</p><p>“I know that I proved a little bit more on my offensive side, but definitely I'm that type of guy where I never feel that it's enough,” Vargas said. “Definitely I want to work a little bit more on my defense.”</p><p>After a surprise 84-win campaign, and even more acutely coming a win shy of playing in the American League Championship Series, the young White Sox are similarly shifting from trying to shock as Vargas did, to trying to level up.</p><p>An offseason that will see players disconnected from the coaching staff due to a nearing lockout provides a challenge for a group that thrived on team chemistry. But Vargas is already planning on hosting teammates at his home in Miami for offseason training, and doesn’t think the burden of expectations will weigh any heavier than those they are already carrying.</p><p>“The best part about this group, we still believe that we could have went to the ALCS,” Vargas said. “We didn't, but from the bottom of the heart we believed that we could do a better job.”</p>

entries.title: The Power of POI, Weaving Literary Genres into a Central Theme and Reinventing the Story of Medea
entries.summary: <p>Jeff Award-winning director Denise Yvette Serna credits her Texas public school roots for a big part of her success in producing, curating and managing performance spaces, stories and soul-stirring experiences.</p><p>Serna, a Bridgeport resident who was born in San Antonio and raised in San Juan, Texas, competed in One-Act Play contests, forensics, improvised theater and extemporaneous speech, as well as in timed linguistics trials. They were all part of the regular curriculum in the public K-12 schools she attended in Pharr-San Juan-Alamo Independent School District.</p><p>“When I was in eighth grade, I had a teacher who sat me down and told me, ‘You are good at this. It’s OK to be good at this,’” Serna said, recalling her middle-school theater teacher Lisa Moreno’s life-altering words when Serna was 14.</p><p></p><p>“She set me on a trajectory,” Serna said of Moreno. “From high school, I wanted to learn to do theatre. I said, ‘I’m going to be an actor.’”</p><p></p><p>Serna fell in love with POI<b> </b>(Program Oral Interpretation) — weaving creative pieces such as a song lyric, a dramatic outtake and an anonymous poem — into a creative whole.</p><p>Her mixture of prose, poetry and drama come together as she co-directs “Mojada” — inspired by Euripides’ Medea — at the Court Theatre in Hyde Park, running March 12 to April 11, 2027.</p><p>At the same time, she is directing “72 Miles to Go” by writer Hilary Bettis at Western Michigan University, and “Woman’s Work” by playwright Elenna Stauffer at Artemisia Theatre’s WeWomen Play Festival of new feminist works, running Nov. 16-18 at Bramble Arts Loft, 5545 N. Clark St.</p><p>Serna started her relationship with “Medea” appropriately enough — with a show staged 12 years ago with Inappropriate Theatre Company and Crush Dance Collective at Transamoeba Studios in the South Loop. Transamoeba was, at the time, an art studio and DIY space where Serna and the two companies presented their immersive production, “La Chingada.”</p><p>“We kept the address a secret, and walked patrons from a meet-up point at Roosevelt Road and State Street,” said Serna, who at the time lived in an artists’ housing co-op called The Roost in the Rogers Park neighborhood.</p><p>Serna submitted the work as the final submission of her master’s thesis when she earned an MFA in Theatre Directing from East 15 Acting School in London.</p><p>She then focused on “La Llorona,” a Latin American legend of the violated mother figure that Serna said “has taken space within my consciousness as long as I’ve had one.”</p><p>The legend has La Llorona wandering riverbanks stealing children and finally, drowning herself.</p><p>Serna delved into dramaturgical research and found similar stories throughout the world in songs, poetry, art pieces and other plays.</p><p>“I find it so sad that she lived a whole life of love and loss; a whole legend, and yet the only thing she ever said was, ‘Ay, mis hijos,’” Serna said.</p><p>Serna’s play allowed for La Llorona to evolve from colonial trauma to the single woman of La Chingada.</p><p>Serna questioned why audiences have in the past condemned La Llorona, a woman who legend says could be heard crying at night in Tenochtitlan (now Mexico City) in 1509, and yet sympathized with Medea, who legend says betrayed and killed her own family to help and be with the Greek hero Jason, who stole the Golden Fleece.</p><p>Serna’s interpretation let La Llorona speak only through movement until the final moments of the play to emphasize her finally owning her own voice.</p><p>Serna’s career continued to evolve, as she accepted a fellowship in 2015 at Steppenwolf Theatre Company. She then worked in development and audience engagement before becoming front-of-house manager.</p><p>In 2018, while directing Lauren Gunderson’s “The Revolutionists” at Strawdog Theatre Company, and working as assistant director at Steppenwolf Theatre Co. with Sandra Marquez, Serna left her job as fulltime house manager.</p><p>Her breakthrough came in 2022, when she directed Brian Quijada’s musical “Somewhere Over the Border” for Teatro Vista. It won three Jeff Awards, including best director of a midsize musical for Serna.</p><p>Now, Serna is co-directing MacArthur Genius Award-winning playwright Luis Alfaro’s “Mojada” with Wendy Mateo, artistic director of Teatro Vista Productions. Serna is an artistic collective member at the Latine-led Teatro Vista.</p><p>In Chicano playwright and performance artist Alfaro’s version, Mojada, an undocumented Mexican seamstress, has survived a harrowing odyssey to Chicago from Mexico. This experience brings about a transformation in Medea. She is faced with a difficult choice: Not IF she will survive, but how.</p><p>The retelling of a 2,800-year-old Greek tragedy — elements of the Medea character were circulated during the Iliad and the Odyssey — deals with enduring truths behind the mythology, and, Serna says, how she wants audiences to see their own conceptions of the story.</p><p>“Our species has a long history of migration patterns, in which we search for safety, home, ecological reciprocity, and a legible future for our lineage,” Serna said. “We are a species capable of incredible devotion, intelligence and compassion. We are also capable of deceit, cruelty, exploitation, and irreversible destruction.</p><p>“I hope that this version of Medea’s story reminds you of every woman you have ever known,” she said. “What we see. What we endure. What we are capable of.</p><p>“I hope that you are exposed to the complex issues and conversations related to the experiences of migrants and immigrants in Chicago.</p><p>“When this play premiered in Chicago in 2013, we did not anticipate the escalation of xenophobia, antiblackness, and state-sanctioned violence that we would experience in this decade.</p><p>“Mojada immerses us in the heart of Pilsen, where multiple generations of americanos find themselves today,” Serna said. “It has become more than just a Chicano story. Even as I am so proud and excited to bring in authentic expressions of Mexican, Indigenous and Chicano lifestyles into the piece, I am even more excited to raise the question: “Are we going to let ourselves be fooled into thinking we aren’t capable of immense creativity, revelation and power?</p><p>“Are we going to turn our backs on people who look and live just like us because othering them makes us feel safe?”</p><p>Serna lives out her philosophy that theatre is an “act of service” by co-running with Dulce Morales the Global Hive Laboratories’ and Cedillo’s Fresh Produce’s The People’s Pot & Pantry, a free pantry and community meal provider she supplies from Dulce’s farm in the South Side Englewood neighborhood.</p><p>“Teatro Vista Productions is the Midwest’s only Latine-led Equity theatre company, and we are bringing experimental forms, communication technology, and multidisciplinary expertise to every production we mount,” Serna said.</p><p>“Mojada will be a chance to see what we do when we have institutional support and nationwide reach,” she said. “Our ideas and our aesthetic, paired with phenomenal women in leadership, position us as a powerful force in the performing arts for the 21st century.</p><p>“This production is not one to miss.”</p>
entries.author: Sandra Guy

entries.title: Director Explores Life’s Dark Side So Audiences Can Better See the Light
entries.summary: <p>Chicago-area community theater director Meg C. James has emerged as a paradigm shifter. She wants you to squirm.</p><p>That’s why her audiences will see the dark side of what they thought was a predictable play — all to ensure they experience life in its entirety and, ultimately, appreciate the light.</p><p>“We need to face that sometimes life isn’t always going to be good and that’s OK,” said James, a native of Lodi, New Jersey, a borough northwest of New York City, who was raised on Broadway shows and who first attended professional theater arts camp at 13.</p><p>Her arts immersion felt natural.</p><p>“I’m Filipino, and music, art and dance are deeply embedded in our culture,” she said. “My mom has seen everything I’ve done [on stage].”</p><p>Yet James noticed a lack of diversity, with few women of color playing the lead. So now, as a director, she takes care to issue a detailed casting description to ensure roles for people other than Caucasian.</p><p>By the time James was in high school, she felt a new urge, spurred on by her paternal grandmother.<b> </b></p><p>James’s trajectory shifted when she watched helplessly as her grandmother struggled with heart pain, and, ultimately suffered a heart attack.</p><p>James once again saw discrimination in the form of medical neglect.</p><p>Indeed, she bridled at medical professionals ignoring her grandmother and telling her grandmother that she was being ‘overly dramatic’ when she experienced heart pain.</p><p>So James earned a bachelor’s degree in nursing and a master’s degree in nurse education from Purdue University Northwest in Hammond, Indiana.</p><p>Like many local theater actors, engineers and directors, James works fulltime at a more lucrative, technologically focused career: She’s a clinical informaticist specialist.</p><p>“My job is to be the bridge between Information Technology (IT) and its end users,” she said, noting that she specializes in workflow analysis for pediatrics and labor delivery. “I make nurses’ lives easier so they can spend more time bedside.”</p><p>James found herself pulled back into the theater when a friend of hers at Purdue University Northwest urged her to audition for a play at the small school theater.</p><p>COVID intervened, but the theater bug had bitten.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a the Genesius Theatre in Hammond.</p><p>Though James figured she would act and sing, she found herself drawn toward directing. And for the past four years, she has served primarily as the assistant director or the director in community theater.</p><p>As a result, her eye for the dark side focused on opportunities.</p><p>In the musical Pippin performed by the Genesius Guild in Hammond, James centered the lead character’s struggle to find his life’s meaning — trying roles such as a prince, an artist and a farm hand — around a Midsummer pole, a tall wooden pole decorated with wreaths.</p><p>And while Pippin dressed in blue and the Leading Player in red, the rest of the cast who danced around the pole were dressed in white and wore flower-wreaths around their heads.</p><p>The audience comes to realize the white-robed group, who encourage Pippin to harm himself, are cult members who are purposely being sinister.</p><p>“I feel like even if there’s dark, you can find something light,” James said. “Whenever there’s a sunset, there’s a sunrise. You can always find something good somewhere.”</p><p>Her next show, “Avenue Q,” coming up Dec. 3-13<b><u> </u></b>at the GhostLight Theater<b> </b>in Benton Harbor,<b> </b>Michigan,<b> </b>tells the story of a recent college graduate named Princeton, who moves into a shabby New York apartment all the way out on Avenue Q.</p><p>James, 32, of Winfield, between Crown Point and Valparaiso in Northwest Indiana, commutes to the Michigan stage while being mom to a 4-year-old boy and a 2-year-old girl. She commutes 90 minutes each way to the rehearsals.</p><p>But James is grateful that her sacrifices feed off each other.</p><p>“My director told me that when we did our first table read for Avenue Q, you looked at Allison, age 18, with so much love,” she said. “I said, ‘I’m a mom. I want people to know I love them. I want to listen to them.’</p><p>“That’s changed me. I have become more empathetic,” she said. “I love being a mom. I’m super grateful to be able to take those experiences and apply it to theater.”</p>

entries.title: It's (almost) Thanksgiving. What are you grateful for?
entries.summary: <p>You won the lottery.</p><p>You do know that, right? Start with that initial splash of "seminal wet," to use Walt Whitman's memorable phrase (one of several he coined for this particular substance. I smile to see Whitman included among Donald Trump's proposed National Garden of American Heroes. He wouldn't include Harvey Fierstein. It's because these Republicans don't read. "Leaves of Grass" could be titled "Tales of the City, 1855." It's a gay romp, in places).</p><p>Sorry, where was I? A hundred million sperm in a teaspoon of fatherstuff, to again cite Whitman, where only one — the future you — fought its way past all the others. A mad, tail-wriggling sprint over a few inches — still quite a distance for a tadpole 1/500th of an inch long. The equivalent of an adult swimming several miles. </p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-660000" name="module-660000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Opinion bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Opinion</h2></div> </div><p>Had another wriggled faster, you would have never existed, and some other, different person, at least genetically, would have taken your place. You would have ended up ... nowhere.</p><p>Instead, you beat 100 million-to-one odds by just showing up, and since then have, through a combination of skill, smarts, and plain dumb luck, avoided the daily winnowing. You did not join those kindergarteners blundering dreamily in front of a school bus. Or those high schoolers who chug 12 beers and drive into a tree. Or the sophomores surrendering to despair. Or adults who bite the baited hook of disease and are yanked out of this world long before their time.</p><p>Thanksgiving is Thursday. The emphasis is usually on what we are given. A luscious holiday feast, for starters, that most enjoy through the efforts of others. To the general bounty of our lives the other 364 days a year. Days that begin with glorious orange and yellow sunrises, the dawn breaking clear, then progress punctuated by colorful birds and strong cups of hot coffee. All the way to golden sunsets. Then the stars come out, twinkling emissaries from the past. The moon was full Tuesday night, the same moon that Julius Caesar, George Washington and Elvis Presley contemplated.</p><p>There is so much to give thanks for.</p><p>An odd word, "thank" — look it up in the Oxford English Dictionary, and its roots disappear a thousand years ago into Middle English and Teutonic, tangled with the word "think."</p><p>That's apt. Thankfulness is bound up in thought. It's an attitude, though we obscure that by giving thanks for specific benefits — for this good dinner, for that compliment, for being passed the stuffing — so much so that we forget that gratitude is also an attitude, a general condition, an overarching mindset, the face we turn toward the world, no matter what expression the world is showing us at the moment.</p><p>Gratitude is not based on what you have. Rather it's the dog you hunt with. You unleash gratitude, say, "Go get 'em, boy," and see what he brings back, twitching. You must scan the woods for reasons. It takes effort. I remind myself, in the morning, to find something to be grateful for today. Even realities that at first seem something to complain about rather than appreciate. Growing old comes to mind. And my body falling apart. Not fun, but then, my friend Tony will never grow older than he was last year. And my friend Jeff's body fell apart in one crash in Michigan. Honestly, I'll take the slow version of both, and be grateful for them, as privileges denied many.</p><p>I recommend you do the same. Whatever ride you are on, it took the universe 13.8 billion years to cough you up into consciousness, and untold billions will pass after you snap off like a popped light bulb. Might as well enjoy it. And gratitude is the key to the door of happiness.</p><p>I know of an organization whose members are often in a state of disarray. Their personal lives are a miserable mess. They've torched their relationships. Wrecked their health, traded the glorious bounty of the world for staring into the outhouse hole of various addictions. And now even those are rudely denied them.</p><p>Yet they regularly speak of gratitude, for the small spark of a good life they've set among wet tinder and are huffing on with all their might. For whatever good is going on, and if none comes to mind, for the hope of better days to come. Gratitude is the rope they're tossed, and they grab at it.</p><p>So this Thanksgiving, whoever you are, I extend to you a lifeline. Whether or not you take it, well, I'm grateful for you considering the offer, and for you reading this today and throughout the year. I'm on vacation next week, finishing a book, but I've got one more column Friday, and am thankful for that, too. Happy Thanksgiving.</p>
entries.author: Neil Steinberg

entries.title: Bears QB Caleb Williams looks to get back to Goldilocks Zone in potential shootout with Lions
entries.summary: <p>Coming off the best three-game stretch of his career, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> quarterback Caleb Williams slipped into a rut. The way he played the last two games — wins over opponents with a combined 6-14 record — won’t be good enough to beat a good team, and the Lions will prove it Thursday if he doesn’t rediscover what worked.</p><p>Williams was brilliant in those three games and looked like the quarterback the Bears imagined he could become when they paired him with coach <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/11/20/bears-coach-ben-johnsons-straight-talk-changes-the-conversation-at-halas-hall" >Ben Johnson</a>. He was perceptive, quick and almost unstoppable as he ran Johnson’s offense to near-perfection.</p><p>He seemed to get ahead of himself, though, after a hot start against the Buccaneers two games ago and became too carefree as he threw four interceptions. Then, coming out of the bye week, he appeared to overcorrect as he looked tentative at times and held the ball more than usual.</p><p>Williams needs a reset. The key to getting back to how he looked when he vaulted himself into the MVP race is getting out of his own head.</p><p>That’s not necessarily how he would phrase it, but he did think he was off against the Saints when it came to pouncing on easy openings their defense offered him and overall decisiveness.</p><p>“I was just getting through the reads maybe too fast, or maybe a little too slow, and you're missing opportunities,” he said after a walk-through Tuesday. “Just pulling the trigger, being decisive — that's something I always harp on.</p><p>“I’ve got to be decisive, deliver a good ball — all the things that I was doing [in that three-game stretch].”</p><p>Johnson wasn’t worried by Williams’ game against the Saints. He acknowledged that he was “up and down,” but arrived at “solid” for an overall appraisal.</p><p>He and offensive coordinator Press Taylor both labeled Williams’ interception as a great play by defensive end Carl Granderson, who jumped at the line of scrimmage to tip the pass and send it floating for an easy catch by linebacker Danny Stutsman, rather than a bad choice by Williams. He was throwing to Luther Burden, who was wide open for a first down, and operating the play exactly as designed.</p><p>Johnson also pushed back Tuesday on a question about whether Williams was hesitant.</p><p>Williams finished 15-for-23 passing (65.2%) for 181 yards with two touchdown passes and an interception for a 100.1 passer rating. There were years when the Bears were desperate for a quarterback to play that well, but standards have changed.</p><p>He wasn’t bad by any means, but it’s hard to imagine the Bears beating teams like the Lions — the Jaguars and Bills are coming up, too — with so little production in the passing attack. Being efficient and avoiding turnovers are virtuous, but that’s not enough. The Bears need Williams to be a dynamic difference maker.</p><p>“When the shots are there, take them and we’ve got to hit them,” he said, referring specifically to a miss on a deep throw Sunday to rookie wide receiver Zavion Thomas in which the two weren’t on the same wavelength. “You’ve got to hit those because it starts racking up throughout the game. When you hit those super explosives, your [production] goes up.”</p><p>The effect of hitting or missing those plays will be very obvious against the Lions. The issue isn’t so much Williams beating their defense, but keeping up with their offense.</p><p>The Lions’ run over the last five seasons has been powered by quarterback Jared Goff and a host of elite offensive weapons — developments shaped by Johnson when he was on staff before taking this job. Defense has been their weak spot throughout, and this season is no different.</p><p>The Lions are 15th in total defense, the best they’ve been during this era, but that likely will slide after losing Aidan Hutchinson, one of the NFL’s top defensive ends, to a season-ending knee injury. They’re shaky against the pass and were managing that deficiency with a fierce pass rush, which is harder to do without Hutchinson.</p><p>The offense, though, is decidedly ahead of the Bears, and that’s why this is going to be a track meet. Williams must outpunch a Lions’ offense averaging 28.8 points per game, and that group totaled 67 points and 880 total yards the last two weeks against the Patriots and Bucs.</p><p>“I've gone into every game of my career thinking that it's going to take us putting up 40 points,” he said. “My mindset is always that each drive, each play, can be a touchdown. It can be momentum-changing for us. It can be the game-sealing touchdown. Let's go out there and treat it that way."</p><p>Williams has tended to rise to the moment, and this is a huge one as the teams, both 8-2, wrestle to control the NFC North. He’s 0-4 against the Lions, and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/11/04/bears-qb-caleb-williams-is-once-again-the-talk-of-the-nfl-but-hes-controlling-the-conversation-now" target="_blank" >as someone constantly seeking sources of motivation</a>, it’s certainly in his mind that Johnson is still looking for his first win against his former team.</p><p>The best way to deliver for his coach is to run the offense as intended.</p><p>At this point in their time together, Williams is fully fluent in Johnson’s play designs and calls and needs to get back to maximizing them with sharp decision makings, accurate passes and the right balance of patience and assertiveness.</p><p>Not too long ago, he did that beautifully. The Bears badly need to see it again.</p>

entries.title: ICC cuts $53 million from Illinois American Water rate-hike proposal
entries.summary: <p>Nearly 350,000 Illinois American Water customers will see smaller increases to their water bills after the Illinois Commerce Commission cut roughly $53 million from a requested rate-hike. </p><p>The utility earlier this year had originally proposed a $142.4 million increase to rates before amending the proposal to $127 million. The commission's ruling cut roughly 41% from the requested rate-hike, making the approved increase $74 million. </p><p>“Any decision impacting Illinoisans’ bills is not a small one. The ICC’s responsibility is to balance the interests of Illinois’ utilities and their consumers, and the increase approved today reflects a fair and reasonable determination based on carefully considered modeling,” said Illinois Commerce Commission Chairman Doug Scott.</p><p>In addition to cutting the proposed rate increase, the decision also approves a 9.67% return on equity, a reduction from the utility’s requested 10.75% return as well as from the utility’s current 9.84% return, according to the commission. </p><p>Illinois American serves 148 communities across the state, including some in suburban Chicago. It operates the water delivery systems in those communities, along with 18 water treatment plants and 17 wastewater treatment facilities around the state.</p><p>The Illinois Commerce Commission ruled against Illinois American’s two-step rate hike proposal, deeming it "unreasonable" during a special meeting Tuesday morning where the final order was given. </p><p>But the commission approved the utility's proposal to separate residential and non-residential customer wastewater rates "because it better reflects cost causation principles," though it's also clarified that the proposal "does not appropriately consider" those principles.</p><p>"We appreciate the Commission’s thorough review of the case. At this time, Illinois American Water staff is carefully reviewing the Commission’s decision to determine its impact on customers and the company," Illinois American Water said in a statement. </p><p>Under the original $127 million increase proposal, rates for customers using 3,500 gallons of water per month would have increased an average of $10 a month, while wastewater customers would've seen an average increase of $23 a month, the Citizens Utility Board said, citing previous estimates by the utility. The exact impact of the new, lower increase isn't yet clear.</p><p>In June, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/money/2026/06/03/consumer-advocacy-groups-oppose-illinois-american-water-rate-hike-acquisition" target="_blank" >consumer advocates</a> wanted Illinois American Water to cut its proposed $142.4 million rate hike by 38%, saying the company was seeking exorbitant profits.</p><p>"Cutting Illinois American Water’s proposed increase by about 41 percent represents real progress in holding this utility accountable, but we know it’s little comfort to customers who have been struggling with escalating water bills for years while the utility’s profits keep growing," the Citizens Utility Board said in a statement. "The ICC alone can’t ease the suffering of private water customers in Illinois — we urgently need to reform the state water laws that have allowed Illinois American to plunder its customers."</p><p>Illinois American’s proposal was submitted after the Illinois Commerce Commission approved a separate <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/consumer-affairs/2024/12/07/utility-illinois-american-water-will-increase-water-rates-in-2025" target="_blank" >$110 million rate increase for the company for 2025</a>.</p><p>Tuesday's ruling came days after state regulators <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/business/2026/11/19/illinois-commerce-commission-peoples-gas-rate-hike-slashed" target="_blank" >slashed nearly $104 million</a> from a rate hike requested by Peoples Gas.</p>

entries.title: U.S. stockpile of bomb-making chemical lead azide to be detonated Wednesday morning at Iowa plant, Army says
entries.summary: <p>Middletown, Iowa — The U.S. Army plans to detonate the nation’s entire stockpile of lead azide in Iowa on Wednesday morning, warning that the dangerously degrading bomb-making chemicals could otherwise explode at any time.</p><p>“Inaction is no longer an option,” said Maj. Gen. Eric Shirley, the Army’s leader of the operation.</p><p>Officials on Tuesday warned nearby residents to be ready to evacuate to avoid toxic dust in the air while also trying to assure them that barriers around the blast zone should limit much of the plume.</p><p>“We don’t believe that the public should be in a panic,” said Acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle. “Our goal is to keep as much of it as we can here on our Iowa Army Ammunition plant to prevent it from traveling.</p><p>The controlled detonation of roughly five tons of degraded lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown has set off concerns about potential health and environmental effects and frustration over a lack of information. Experts have advised the stockpile will become more volatile as temperatures cool in the coming days.</p><p>The Army rescheduled the detonation in southeastern Iowa to Wednesday because of more favorable wind conditions and to allow more time for extra safety measures, according to the court filing by the government.</p><p>Detonation of the 68 barrels had been set for last Friday. The Army said they need to blow up the stockpile to prevent a possible chain-reaction explosion, which would be more dangerous.</p><h3>Army takes steps to limit plume</h3><p>Officials overseeing the plan say the wind on Wednesday is expected to blow southwest, away from nearby Burlington, a city of nearly 25,000 people along the Mississippi River.</p><p>The Army released new maps Tuesday showing the likely trajectory of the plume traveling toward Missouri. Plans for an earlier detonation had the plume headed north and possibly west into Illinois.</p><p>An emergency notification sent to cellphones Tuesday morning said the detonation was planned for 9 a.m. Wednesday and that some people within 5 miles southwest of the plant may be evacuated.</p><p>The “imminent threat alert” told those up to 20 miles away to remain indoors with windows closed “to avoid airborne lead dust, noise and vibration.”</p><p>The Army has set up additional “blast barriers” around the bunkers where the lead azide will be detonated, and to apply ballistic gels and foams to absorb the lead dust. It also plans to douse the materials with thousands of gallons of water.</p><p>“We’ve taken every viable solution and considered it,” Telle said. “In every instance, the answer is controlled detonation is safest.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-180000" </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Laura Bargfeld/Associated Press</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3>Federal court approved the detonation</h3><p>The Army won approval for the detonation from the federal appeals court in a saga that sowed confusion and included an unusual twist from President Donald Trump.</p><p>A court said Monday that the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency adequately incorporated safeguards in an emergency permit to minimize the dispersal of dust. Those conditions address the concerns of environmental groups that sued to stop the detonation, the court said.</p><p>The court pointed to barriers put up around the area where the barrels are stored along with weather restrictions.</p><p>The judges said the record also reflected that the Army evaluated “a full range” of alternatives, including using other chemicals to neutralize the lead azide and thermal treatment but determined detonation was safest.</p><p>In an twist, Trump, commander-in-chief of the Army, said in a social media post that besides court approval, he wanted Gov.-elect Rob Sand to OK the detonation. Sand, a Democrat who doesn’t take office until January, has said the decision is fully up to the Trump administration.</p><h3>Blast was planned for last week</h3><h3></h3><p>The Army has changed the detonation date three times following an outpouring of public concern.</p><p>Environmentalists sued last week to stop the detonation at the site, about 90 miles south of Cedar Rapids. The court temporarily halted the permit, prompting the Army to argue it didn’t need authorization after all, given that it was an emergency.</p><p>An attorney for the environmentalists emphasized their legal challenge centers on the validity of the EPA permit, not the Army’s decision to move forward with the detonation under the emergency provision.</p><p>Earthjustice managing attorney Rachel Rintelmann said the lawsuit has alerted the public to the threat. Iowa Gov. Kim Reynolds activated the state emergency management office on Friday. The state also created a website for information about the operation.</p><p>Reynolds said Tuesday that, after speaking with military leaders, including Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, she supports the planned detonation.</p><p>“I trust the Army will do everything in its power to protect the people who could be affected,” Reynolds said.</p><h3>Residents in limbo ahead of detonation</h3><p>Some residents near Middletown have been sealing windows and doors to keep out any lead dust from the detonation. Others living farther away were raising concerns about the possible paths the plume could take depending on the wind.</p><p>Officials have recommended that people stay indoors when the detonation happens and clean off outdoor surfaces with water afterward to limit exposure to any lead particles.</p><p>Middletown Mayor Rodney Johnson said the detonation must take place “so we can move on with our lives.”</p><p>“Improper storage and disposal is where things go wrong,” he said on social media.</p><p>Missouri Gov. Mike Kehoe said state agencies are working to establish additional monitoring of air and water quality, public health and agriculture resources.</p><h3>Army says plans intended to avoid something worse</h3><h3></h3><p>In court filings, Army Col. Aaron Teller, a munitions emergency response specialist, said that less liquid inside the barrels means the solution is more susceptible to freezing, which increases the risk of an explosive chain reaction.</p><p>Staff at the Iowa ammunition plant notified the EPA about the barrels in March. The Army then assembled experts in munitions chemistry, engineering and environmental safety to come up with a plan.</p><p>According to EPA documents, alternatives to a detonation were considered. But officials said handling the drums would increase the probability of an accidental, fatal blast.</p><p><i>Contributing: Associated Press writers Konstantin Toropin in Washington, D.C.; Scott Bauer in Madison, Wisconsin; Jacques Billeaud in Phoenix; Christopher Weber in Los Angeles and Dave Collins in Hartford, Connecticut. Montoya Bryan reported from Albuquerque, New Mexico.</i></p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/environment/2026/11/20/the-army-plans-to-detonate-a-toxic-lead-compound-near-the-illinois-iowa-border-heres-what-to-know" >The Army plans to detonate a toxic lead compound near the Illinois-Iowa border: What to know</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/environment/2026/11/23/trump-orders-the-army-not-to-detonate-bomb-making-chemicals-in-iowa-without-court-approval" >Federal appeals court clears way for U.S. Army to detonate degraded bomb-making material in Iowa</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: After another fumble, what do Bears do with D'Andre Swift now?
entries.summary: <p>The first time D’Andre Swift fumbled this season, he likely cost the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> a win. The running back dropped the ball at the goal line in a Week 2 game the Bears lost to the Vikings by six.</p><p>The second time Swift fumbled, he might have cost Kyle Monangai more than a month of game action. After he fumbled in the third quarter against the Jets, coach Ben Johnson benched him in favor of Monangai, who ran 18 times the rest of the game, totaling 30 overall, and then missed five games with turf toe.</p><p>The third time Swift fumbled — in the fourth quarter Sunday against the Saints while holding an 11-point lead — he was benched again. So now what? What does Ben Johnson do with his best running back? Does he not start? More importantly, does he not finish?</p><p>The Bears’ run game has struggled enough without the head coach having to ask himself whether he trusts Swift to hang onto the ball.</p><p>Johnson isn’t in the mood to belabor the issue — Sunday, using one word, he said he didn’t need to say anything to Swift. Tuesday, he elaborated, only barely.</p><p>“He just needs to hold on to the ball,” he said, “and we'll be fine.”</p><p>Johnson’s actions could speak louder. Monangai had six ineffective carries in his return from turf toe Sunday. Salvon Ahmed, who was promoted from the practice squad a day earlier, ran six times for 33 yards and provided a speed burst the Bears had been missing. Tuesday, Johnson said Ahmed has taken “full advantage” of his opportunity and could be used against the Lions. </p><p>Still, the Bears must continue to treat Swift as their first option. He's too vital to their run and pass games to be mothballed, even if he's one more fumble away from a full-blown crisis. Swift has fumbled three times in 10 games this season. Only three running backs — the Bills’ James Cook, the Giants’ Cam Skattebo and the Colts’ Jonathan Taylor — have more. The fumbles are now part of Swift’s scouting report — opposing teams figure to keep hacking away at the football.</p><p>Swift said the same when asked by the Sun-Times about his fumbles.</p><p>“Keep doing the work,” he said. “Trying my best to keep two hands on it as I’m falling to the ground. Defenders are doing a better job of just attacking it.”</p><p>He hasn’t been a fumbler for most of his career. Entering this season, he had 13 in 89 games — or a fumble rate about half that of this season. He had two apiece in his first two seasons with the Bears.</p><p>Swift — who is 14<sup>th</sup> in the NFL 62.7 rushing yards per game and fifth with 10 rushing touchdowns — said there’s no extra added motivation playing the Lions, who traded him to the Eagles in April 2023.</p><p>“No added extra or anything,” he said. “Just go play ball.”</p><p>Johnson spent the bye week trying to find ways to unlock a rushing offense that was far more persistent than it was explosive. Early returns were less than satisfying; while the Bears totaled their most rushing yards since Week 4, their running backs averaged just 3.8 yards per carry. The Bears are still looking for a breakthrough.</p><p>“It's a commitment to the principles that we have in terms of bringing it to life,” Johnson said. “We have a vision for what we want it to look like. It takes all 11 to bring it to life.</p><p>“We continue to harp on it. Like I said, like everything, things pop up over the course of the season that you want to continue to fix and get better at. The more you emphasize it, the better you get at it.”</p><p>The same goes for Swift’s fumbles.</p><p>“Just hold the ball,” Swift said. “There ain’t nothing really else, but the work.”</p>

entries.title: Johnson pitches vacant land tax, doubles down on head tax — a budget idea his opposition warns won’t fly
entries.summary: <p>Mayor Brandon Johnson on Tuesday amended his proposed 2027 budget, introducing a new tax on vacant, privately owned land in an effort to close a $75 million spending plan gap.</p><p>But the revised proposal leaves intact Johnson's <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/10/20/mayor-brandon-johnson-failed-corporate-head-tax-resurrected-proposed-budget" >proposed corporate head tax</a> that remains the biggest obstacle to securing City Council support. A majority of alderpersons have urged Johnson to drop the head tax and apply the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/11/02/city-council-mayor-johnson-defeat-75m-parking-meter-windfall-stonepeak-partners" >$75 million up-front payment</a> from Stonepeak Partners, the New York investment firm that acquired Chicago’s parking meters, to the 2026 budget as an extra payment to chip away at the city’s $36 billion pension crisis.</p><p></p><p>“The mayor has done half of his assignment. Half of his assignment is putting forward a budget,” said Ald. Gilbert Villegas (36th). “The other half of the assignment is putting forward a budget that can get votes. Right now, the votes are not there.”</p><p>Villegas is part of the Budget Accountability Coalition, a group of Council members that have pushed Johnson to revise his proposal. <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/09/28/city-council-opposition-pre-election-budget-battle-mayor-brandon-johnson" target="_blank" >Twenty-nine alderpersons previously signed a letter </a>asking the mayor to remove the corporate head tax, avoid relying on anticipated state funding and direct the Stonepeak $75 million windfall toward pension payments in the 2026 budget.</p><p>In a statement Tuesday, the coalition said Johnson had not incorporated its recommendations, arguing businesses and working families should not be expected to shoulder the city's deficit.</p><p>“We asked for a whole chicken and we got like a nugget out of that,” said Ald. Bill Conway (34th), who signed the coalition's letter.</p><p>“As long as there is a head tax in the budget, there will not be enough votes to pass the budget,” Conway said. “We made that clear in a letter the majority of City Council signed to the mayor before the budget was released, and we have made that clear in countless public and private meetings since.”</p><p>The corporate head tax would apply to companies with more than 125 employees. Johnson said it would affect about 2.8% of Chicago corporations and includes a hiring credit for businesses that recruit workers from historically disinvested communities.</p><p>But Conway disputed the administration's characterization of the tax as narrowly targeting large corporations. Based on the administration's revenue estimate of roughly $113 million, Conway said the proposed $25 monthly head tax would affect approximately 30% of Chicago's workforce.</p><p>“So it's hardly some tax that just hits the creme de la creme of big wealthy businesses,” Conway said. “Something that hits a third of our workforce nearly is clearly a widespread tax on jobs.”</p><p>A <a class="Link" href="https://bpb-us-w2.wpmucdn.com/voices.uchicago.edu/dist/8/3495/files/2026/11/Chicago_EET.pdf" target="_blank" >University of Chicago report</a> released Monday also raised concerns about the tax's potential impact on mid-sized businesses. Villegas said the findings reinforced his concerns that the tax could discourage employers from hiring in Chicago.</p><p></p><p>Johnson defended retaining the tax, arguing corporations should contribute more toward city services rather than forcing cuts to programs residents rely on.</p><p>“It's clear the people of Chicago want us to challenge corporations," Johnson said, "to put more skin in the game."</p><p>He said a hiring credit would encourage companies to create employment opportunities in historically disinvested communities.</p><p></p><p>The revised proposal also introduces a $1,000 tax on privately owned vacant land, which the administration estimates would generate $12 million. The measure is intended to encourage development of unused parcels, with exemptions for open spaces serving neighborhood purposes, including community gardens and green spaces.</p><p>The administration also wants to increase vacant building registration fees, which would generate an estimated $1.2 million. Private owners would pay $150 to register vacant buildings and $50 for six-month renewals. Fees for vacant storefronts would rise to $200 every six months, while real estate-owned properties would face $1,000 fees every six months.</p><p>Conway questioned the administration's decision to introduce development incentives while retaining a tax he said could discourage job growth.</p><p>“You have this big other thing that disincentivizes job growth, and so why don't you get rid of that piece of it?” Conway said. “So it felt like he kept in the one anti-growth thing and sort of put something else in by saying it promotes growth. So I thought that was a contradictory message.”</p><p>Johnson also proposed adding positions within the Finance Department to pursue unpaid revenue. Villegas criticized the expansion, arguing the city should be making government leaner and more efficient as it grapples with a deficit.</p><p></p><p></p><p></p><p></p><p>Johnson said he remains committed to negotiating with council members before the Dec. 31 budget deadline to avoid a government shutdown, arguing that cuts would threaten city services, libraries and housing programs.</p><p>But with alderpersons continuing to identify the corporate head tax as a deal breaker, the mayor faces a familiar challenge: finding a budget that not only closes the city's deficit, but can also secure enough votes to pass.</p><p>“The consequences of failing to reach an agreement are too grave for any of us to take options off the table,” Johnson said.</p>

entries.title: Bears report: Team claims CB Isaac Yiadom
entries.summary: <p>What happened Tuesday at Halas Hall:</p><h3>Waiver claim</h3><p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> claimed cornerback Isaac Yiadom off waivers. The 30-year-old played for defensive coordinator Dennis Allen in New Orleans and in games for six other teams. Like general manager Ryan Poles, he's a Boston College alum. Yiadom didn’t play on defense over three games for the Commanders this year but appeared on 55 special teams downs.</p><h3>Benedet’s good</h3><p>Left tackle Theo Benedet is on track to play Thursday against the Lions after being a full participant in the Bears' estimated injury report. Benedet hurt his quad Sunday but returned to finish the game. Cornerback Kyler Gordon (shoulder) and running back Roschon Johnson (ankle) remain out.</p><h3>Hicks out</h3><p>The Bears ruled out safety Elijah Hicks for Thursday because of a concussion. He played three defensive snaps and 17 special teams downs on Sunday.</p><p>The Lions announced that defensive tackle Skyler Gill-Howard will miss the rest of the season after hurting his knee while playing fullback Sunday. He had two sacks this season. The Lions also listed cornerback Ennis Rakestraw (shoulder) and edge rusher DJ Wonnum (back) as non-participants on their estimated injury report. Both teams held walk-throughs Tuesday.</p>

entries.title: Cubs spend big, dropping $240 million on early Black Friday haul to add Trevor Rogers, Teruaki Sato
entries.summary: <p>A Black Friday shopping spree came early for the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a>.</p><p>Jed Hoyer’s front office spent big, smashing a favorite narrative of frustrated fans by bringing in two of baseball’s top offseason prizes.</p><p>The haul? <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/11/24/cubs-trevor-rogers-mlb-offseason-free-agents-rumors-pitching-starting-rotation-2027" >Lefty starting pitcher Trevor Rogers</a> and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/11/24/cubs-teruaki-sato-mlb-offseason-free-agents-rumors-outfield-third-base-jed-hoyer-contract-salary" >left-handed hitting Japanese slugger Teruaki Sato</a>, each costing a reported $120 million, Rogers’ deal for five years and Sato’s for six.</p><p>It was a statement by Hoyer & Co. ahead of what’s expected to be a lengthy lockout that’ll put the entire sport on pause. And given the length of the pacts, even if the 2027 season is significantly impacted by the work stoppage, the acquisitions are as much about the Cubs’ future as their present.</p><p>The Cubs are far from done, needing to continue remaking their pitching staff and plug a couple more holes in their lineup.</p><p>But two of the top free agents on the market this winter are coming to the North Side, not a bad follow-up to Hoyer’s signing of Alex Bregman an offseason ago, when he brought in the two-time World Series champion on a $175 million deal.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">It’s not baseball weather, as is apparent from all these leaves on the ground, but the Cubs are making news anyway. Here’s a couple two tree things on a big day for the North Siders. <a href="https://x.com/Suntimes?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">@Suntimes</a> <a href="https://x.com/suntimes_sports?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">@suntimes_sports</a> <a href="https://t.co/HIRGGMImkE">pic.twitter.com/HIRGGMImkE</a></p>— Vinnie Duber (@VinnieDuber) <a href="https://x.com/VinnieDuber/status/2125341496425529709?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">November 24, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>Bregman’s track record was longer than either of these guys, sure, but Rogers and Sato are coming off electric seasons, generating hope the Cubs will better compete with the world-champion Brewers in the NL Central.</p><p>Rogers is a former first-round pick and Rookie of the Year runner-up. After returning from the minors in 2025, he was terrific in 18 starts for the Orioles, posting a 1.81 ERA, before turning in a big contract year this past season, particularly good from June on, with a 2.93 ERA over his final 20 outings.</p><p>He’ll shoot right to the top of a work-in-progress Cubs starting staff. All five guys who finished the 2026 campaign in the rotation are free agents, and in-house candidates to fill those vacancies — Justin Steele, Ben Brown and Cade Horton — are coming off significant injuries.</p><p>Rogers provides some immediate stability, but Hoyer has plenty more to do as he tries to elevate the pitching. Rogers is no Jacob Misiorowski, the Brewers’ ace and unanimous Cy Young winner, but the Cubs hope he can beef up a staff that came nowhere close to matching their rivals.</p><p>Sato, meanwhile, is something of a surprise position-player addition in an offseason forecasted to focus on pitching. He arrives from Japan’s Central League as a two-time MVP and the reigning Triple Crown winner, having hit .306 with a .383 on-base percentage to go along with 39 homers and 106 RBIs in 2026.</p><p>Sato mostly played third base with the Hanshin Tigers but played a little outfield and is expected to slot into one of the vacant corner-outfield spots on the Cubs’ roster.</p><p>Another Japanese import, Sato will likely be compared to Seiya Suzuki, if only because he could effectively take his countryman’s place in the Cubs’ lineup. Suzuki was strong in five seasons on the North Side after arriving from Japan, and his possible departure blasts a sizable hole in a lineup that was baseball’s highest scoring last season.</p><p>Sato ought to help with that and could be a middle-of-the-order bat, something that was perhaps not expected to arrive as the team sought pitching upgrades and discussed Matt Shaw and Pedro Ramirez as in-house options in the outfield.</p><p>There are concerns about Sato’s potential to rack up big strikeout numbers, though Munetaka Murakami flourished after similar concerns followed him to the White Sox, finding success in the U.S.</p><p>The Cubs have had luck there, not only with Suzuki but also on the pitching side with Shota Imanaga, perhaps giving reason to think they can get a productive version of Sato.</p><p>Big spending doesn’t automatically equal success. Just ask Skubal’s new employers with the Mets.</p><p>But fans begging the Cubs to act more like a big-market club can consider their wishes fulfilled after this $240 million Black Friday blowout.</p>

entries.title: Chicago developer planning 50 transit-oriented Lake View apartments
entries.summary: <p>Two retail buildings at the border of Lake View and Lincoln Park will be turned into more than 50 apartments, under a transit-oriented development plan.</p><p>JAB Real Estate purchased the properties at 920 and 928 W. Diversey Parkway for $3.8 million, in a deal that closed last week. The Chicago-based firm plans to demolish and redevelop the properties into a five-story, 52-unit apartment building with ground floor retail.</p><p>The site is a few steps away from the Diversey Brown and Purple line station, and due to a city ordinance passed in July, the project will only have eight parking spaces. Fifty-two bicycle spots will also be included.</p><p>“Where the city is most set up to increase density is the train lines, where you don't have to rely on a certain parking ratio,” Joe Smazal, Interra Realty’s senior managing partner and one of the brokers on the sale, said. “There's definitely a little bit more of a public desire, I think, to increase density around train lines.”</p><p>JAB didn’t respond to requests for comment.</p><p>Plans submitted to the city in October<b> </b>show a brick and stone clad building with tall arches. The building will also have 3,200 square feet of retail space, which plans show is for an undisclosed restaurant. The roof will feature an amenity deck and dog run.</p><p>The apartments will include one- and two-bedrooms, as well as one-bedroom units with dens. Of the 52 units, nine will be affordable.</p><p>Smazal said the transit-rich location was a big driver of interest for the property. There were 10 offers, and the property was on the market for less than a month.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-2a0000" name="image-2a0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/28e568f/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3000x1684+0+225/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F2a%2Fcb%2F1492174b407c92b0d2fe4e6bea7e%2Fdiverseyredev-261125-6.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/310e093/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3000x1684+0+225/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F2a%2Fcb%2F1492174b407c92b0d2fe4e6bea7e%2Fdiverseyredev-261125-6.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/3c3acb2/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3000x1684+0+225/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F2a%2Fcb%2F1492174b407c92b0d2fe4e6bea7e%2Fdiverseyredev-261125-6.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="A pedestrian walks by one of the two properties at 920-928 W. Diversey Parkway that will be demolished to make way for a five-story, 52-unit apartment building, with ground floor retail." srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/3c3acb2/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3000x1684+0+225/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F2a%2Fcb%2F1492174b407c92b0d2fe4e6bea7e%2Fdiverseyredev-261125-6.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/5c76e8e/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3000x1684+0+225/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F2a%2Fcb%2F1492174b407c92b0d2fe4e6bea7e%2Fdiverseyredev-261125-6.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/3c3acb2/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3000x1684+0+225/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F2a%2Fcb%2F1492174b407c92b0d2fe4e6bea7e%2Fdiverseyredev-261125-6.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>A pedestrian walks by one of the two properties at 920-928 W. Diversey Parkway that will be demolished to make way for a five-story, 52-unit apartment building, with ground floor retail.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Tyler Pasciak LaRiviere/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Interra marketed the property as an opportunity for transit-oriented development, Smazal said. In addition to the Diversey station, there’s multiple bus lines nearby.</p><p>“You're not adjacent to the train, but it's just at your doorstep. It’s as walkable of a location as you could find,” he said. “We were expecting that it'd be received favorably by developers.”</p><p>Since the city has pushed harder for more housing around transit, Smazal said he’s seen an increased number of sales for transit-oriented development sites.</p><p>A recently passed city <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2025/08/15/parking-requirements-cta-metra-transit-affordable-housing-crisis" >ordinance</a> eliminated parking minimums near public transit, where fewer residents are dependent on cars. The mandate gives developers the option to reduce parking requirements for new construction and rehab housing projects. Depending on a site’s proximity to a CTA or Metra stop, off-street parking can be reduced by up to 50% — or even eliminated.</p><p>Experts say eliminating some parking spots means developers can add more housing units to a project, which would help alleviate the pressures facing Chicago’s housing market. It’s also a boost for developers, at a time when it’s expensive and difficult to build, Smazal said.</p><p>“To be able to have lower parking requirements and some increased density, that's oftentimes what it takes to make a project feasible,” he said.</p><p>Smazal and Interra Realty Director Mark Dykstra, who also brokered the deal, believe the apartments will be in high demand. The property sits between two sought after neighborhoods: <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2026/08/01/cash-properties-sale-open-house-chicago-homebuyers-bidding-wars" >Lincoln Park and Lake View</a>, which are neighborhoods young professionals flock to, Smazal said.</p><p>“Lake View remains one of Chicago’s strongest rental markets. Yet, opportunities to introduce new apartments are increasingly difficult to find,” Dykstra said. “An infill site that can support a midsize building is particularly compelling because it addresses demand for modern housing while keeping the scale of the project more manageable.”</p>

entries.title: Tasa Coffee Roasters sign says shop 'permanently closed'
entries.summary: <p>A popular Latina-run West Humboldt Park coffee roaster has posted a “permanently closed” sign on its door after workers walked off the job over a viral social media post <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/11/23/tasa-coffee-roaster-west-humboldt-immigration-ice-dhs-social-media-worker-walkout" target="_blank" ><u>alleging the shop has ties to ICE</u></a>.</p><p>Tasa Coffee Roasters, at 4136 W. North Ave. in West Humboldt, is owned solely by Jackie Marquez, according to public records in the Nexis database.</p><p>Tasa closed Monday when baristas walked off the job and neighbors threatened to boycott over social media posts that allege that a man with the same name as the owner’s husband, Pierre Marquez, appears in a database of U.S. Department of Homeland Security employees leaked at the end of October. The leaked documents list this individual as having been a supervisory detention and deportation officer at U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.</p><p>WBEZ/Sun-Times has not been able to independently confirm that the man named in the leak is in fact connected to Tasa. Public records reviewed by WBEZ/Sun-Times state that an individual by this name has been employed by DHS, but the agency did not provide direct confirmation of his status or position with the agency.</p><p>A search using the Nexis public records database showed an ICE email address and DHS employment location associated with the man’s name. But WBEZ/Sun-Times could not independently confirm the man is, or was ever, employed by ICE.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure A mother brought her young child to make posters while passing cars honked in support of protesters.</p><p>Neither Jackie nor Pierre have responded to phone calls and texts from a Sun-Times reporter. At the time of publication, neither Marquez had confirmed or denied that Pierre is alleged to be an ICE agent, either.</p><p>Workers posted a statement on Instagram Tuesday afternoon from a local content creator’s page in English and Spanish. It read, in part, “We want to be clear that we were not aware of Pierre’s employment or any of the information that has come to light. … Please understand that our silence on certain questions is not </div></div><p>The controversy attracted at least one mayoral candidate to the coffee shop on Tuesday. Danielle Carter-Walters, a South Sider and founder of Chicago Flips Red, livestreamed to her followers alongside content creator Zoe Leigh.</p><p>“I support small business, and I also support law and order,” Carter-Walters said. “I'm out here to support the small business.”</p><p>Neighbor and local artist Alma DiStefano walked past Tasa on her way home from breakfast Tuesday. She wanted to grab some photos.</p><p>“I've supported this cafe since I've known about it … I believe that they are well aware of how difficult it's been in this neighborhood, being under pressure of Midway Blitz and ICE , so this is really disheartening,” DiStefano said. She added that she’s been going to the coffee shop since it first opened in 2022.</p><p>Several local politicians, including Ald. Jessie Fuentes (26th) have announced on social media that they’ve cut ties with Tasa. Other Latino-owned coffee shops throughout Chicago have made their own posts denouncing the agency for carrying out detentions and deportations across the city.</p>

entries.title: Sky's Elizabeth Williams elected president of WNBA players union
entries.summary: <p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky" >Sky’s</a> Elizabeth Williams has been elected president of the WNBA Players Association, the union announced Tuesday.</p><p>Williams, who has served as the WNBPA secretary since 2018, succeeds Nneka Ogwumike, who retired from the league after the recent season ended. Williams will serve out the final two years of Ogwumike's term that began earlier this year.</p><p>Williams was part of the last two collective bargaining agreement negotiations, including the most recent landmark one that was ratified last spring.</p><p>"I have served in the role of secretary for nearly a decade of my WNBA career, and I feel well equipped to lead players as the landscape of our league continues to grow," said Williams, who has played in the league for the past 12 years. "One of my main goals as president is to increase the engagement of the younger members of this union. I know the value of diverse voices in these conversations. We may not always agree, but I want to make sure every player knows that her voice is being heard. This is the strength of our union."</p><p>Chelsea Gray was elected treasurer for the union and Veronica Burton will replace Williams as secretary.</p><p>Alysha Clark, Ezi Magbegor and Maya Caldwell were elected to the WNBPA's three vice president positions, each carrying a two-year term. It is Clark's second consecutive term on the board.<br></p>
entries.author: AP

entries.title: Man charged in 2025 fatal Dunning DUI crash
entries.summary: <p>A man who was arrested after allegedly driving under the influence in Dunning when he hit a light pole, killing a passenger last February has been charged, according to Chicago police.</p><p>Fernan Millan-Morales, 31, faces felony reckless homicide with a motor vehicle charges and two counts of aggravated DUI leading to death and injury.</p><p>Officers on patrol observed a gray sedan driven by Millan-Morales crash at a high rate of speed into a pole in the 4200 block of North Oak Park Avenue around 2:16 a.m. on <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/dunning/2025/02/08/1-killed-2-injured-in-dunning-crash" target="_blank" ><u>Feb. 8, 2025</u></a>, Chicago police said at the time. A 29-year-old man, a passenger in the vehicle, was pronounced dead at the scene.</p><p>Millan-Morales was taken to Illinois Masonic Medical Center in good condition, according to police. A woman who was also a passenger was taken to Advocate Lutheran General Hospital in Park Ridge in critical condition.</p><p>Millan-Morales is due in court Wednesday.</p>
entries.author: Sun-Times Wire

entries.title: Jaguars-Bears in Week 13 will stay at noon, leaving Texans-Steelers on Sunday night
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" >Bears</a> fans won't lose another noon kickoff when the Jaguars visit Soldier Field on Dec. 6. The NFL decided not to flex the Week 13 game into prime time, leaving Texans-Steelers on NBC's "Sunday Night Football."</p><p>The possibility arose in Week 10, when the Texans lost to fall to 3-6. Had they lost to the Colts in Week 11, the Texans likely would've been out of playoff contention, thus putting their prime-time appearance in jeopardy. But their victory kept them in the hunt, two games behind the seventh-seeded Steelers in the AFC.</p><p>Flexible scheduling aims to remove a bad game from prime time, not put the best game there. Given its playoff implications, Texans-Steelers isn't a bad game, though Jaguars-Bears is arguably a better game as a potential matchup of first-place teams. That said, the Jags don't exactly move the viewership needle.</p><p>Jaguars-Bears still will air on Fox.</p>
entries.author: Jeff Agrest

entries.title: Are Bulls mishandling Matas Buzelis? There's some numbers that say yes
entries.summary: <p>It’s not his shooting.</p><p>The NBA defines clutch time and the stats that accompany it as the final five minutes of a game when the score is within five points.</p><p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bulls" >Bulls’</a> Matas Buzelis has hit 3-of-5 shots in that instance, including 2-of-3 from three-point range this season.</p><p>Last year, he played in 32 clutch games and took a team-high 21 three-pointers, hitting seven (33.3%). That 31-51 team (.378 winning percentage) went 16-16 with Buzelis on the floor in the clutch.</p><p>In the final minute of clutch games last season, Buzelis posted a plus-26 in plus/minus.</p><p>So when he says he feels like he “thrives in crunchtime,” Buzelis isn’t making it up.</p><p>Yet, there Buzelis found himself in the final 4:41 left in Monday’s game with Cleveland, sitting on the bench and watching while most of the reserves held off the Cavaliers for the 122-108 win.</p><p>Coach Tiago Splitter said he sat Buzelis — and Josh Giddey — because of the heavy workload they put in the night before in an overtime loss to Denver. It made sense, especially with Giddey playing over 41 minutes and Buzelis at 38.</p><p>But it’s also happened more than once in the last few weeks. Giddey admitted after the Nuggets loss that Splitter had explained the decisions to him, and they were on the same page. When he was pulled against Cleveland, however, he was visibly ticked off, caught on camera punching a chair.</p><p>Buzelis was also caught on camera, staring onto the court with daggers coming out of his eyes.</p><p>The third-year forward said all the right things after the game, pointing out numerous times that they won the game, “and that’s all that mattered.”</p><p>That doesn’t mean he had a clear understanding of why he’s been pulled each time. A few were warranted, but the Cleveland win was a bit of a head-scratcher. Buzelis had scored 15 first-half points, was a plus-15 heading into third and said he didn’t feel worn down from the night before.</p><p>He got into foul trouble in the third and was a plus-5 in the seven minutes he played in the fourth, despite missing his only shot attempt.</p><p>Splitter was asked about it several different ways after the game, and said, “All (the regulars) played 40 minutes (Sunday) night, and I thought that (the bench) group was doing a good job."</p><p>When it was pointed out that both players seemed to be pretty unhappy with the latest decision, he said, “It’s normal if they get no playing (time) … probably not as happy. But I’m here to coach this basketball team, not to make them happy."</p><p>When pressed again, Splitter said, “Guys, honestly, we won a basketball game; we are talking about the bad things here. Let’s talk about positive, honestly.”</p><p>That doesn’t change the fact that if they do consider Buzelis — and Giddey for that matter — a core foundation piece, trusting him to make key plays and learn how to win games would seemingly be an essential trait in his development.</p><p>A question that was asked of Buzelis.</p><p>“I 100% agree,” Buzelis responded. “As a competitor, as I said before, I want to be in games, and I feel like I should be in the games. That’s the moments I feel like I thrive in crunchtime, so I understand what you’re saying and as I said I want to be in the games.”</p><p>Buzelis did say Splitter has made it clear to him that he needs to improve his defense and rebounding, and the forward also agreed.</p><p>Yes, Splitter was correct, the Bulls did win the game on Monday. This is a rebuild, however, and there’s a long game that’s bigger than the standings.</p><p>Is Buzelis a clutch player? It would be nice to start finding that out.</p>
entries.author: Joe Cowley
